_comment: Patterns shown from Deep behind the commentary notice: details that fit (undesigned coincidences), key words carried through a passage, and repeated scenes. Checked by crates/atlas-cli/src/extra_patterns.rs.

coincidence: two to four sides, each a label, a ref and exact BSB lines from it. keyword: ref (one book), strong (the root's Strong's numbers), in ("In Hebrew", or whose Greek), forms (the BSB words that render it); the build counts the root and marks the forms. scene: parts (id and label) and scenes (who, ref, and the exact BSB words of each part shown).

cites follow config/figure-forms.json: only its quotable works are quoted, the cite list in config/layer-sources.json says who wrote each book's words, and strength is the number of different interpreters cited (3 or more widely agreed, 2 commonly held, 1 some interpreters). Every side and telling lies under some cite's passage. docs/evidence/patterns-*.json records the line each quote was read on.

quotable adds works quoted only here to the list in config/figure-forms.json: J. J. Blunt's Undesigned Coincidences and William Paley's Horae Paulinae, both public domain, read in the CC0 transcriptions verified against their scans.

kinds.label: A detail that fits
kinds.about: One passage mentions a detail in passing, and another, written apart from it, explains it. Writers on this call it an undesigned coincidence: two true accounts of the same events fit together without trying.

kinds.label: A key word
kinds.about: One word comes back again and again through a passage, and carries what the passage is about.

kinds.label: A repeated scene
kinds.about: The same kind of scene is told of different people, with its parts in much the same order, so each telling recalls the others.

patterns.short: Joseph's pleading is told only years later
patterns.about: The account of the pit says nothing of what Joseph said. Years later in Egypt the brothers recall that they saw his anguish when he pleaded with them, a detail the first account leaves out.

sides.label: Joseph thrown into the pit
words: and they took him and threw him into the pit.

sides.label: The brothers remember his pleading
words: We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, but we would not listen.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, in Part I section I of his Undesigned Coincidences, notes that Genesis 37 tells nothing of Joseph's entreaties and that they come out only in the brothers' talk in Genesis 42. Matthew Henry, on Genesis 37:24, fills in Joseph's begging for his life from Genesis 42:21.

cites.quote: we might conclude that he was himself quite passive in the whole transaction ... All these fervent entreaties are sunk in the direct history of the event, and only come out by accident after all.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: Now Joseph begged for his life, in the anguish of his soul ( Gen 42:21 ), entreated, by all imaginable endearments, that they would be content with his coat and spare his life.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Jacob's refusal over Benjamin took a long time
patterns.about: Jacob refuses to let Benjamin go, and the account moves straight on. Only Judah's later words show how long the struggle lasted: they could have gone to Egypt and back twice in the time.

sides.label: Jacob refuses
words: My son will not go down there with you, for his brother is dead, and he alone is left.

sides.label: Judah on the delay
words: If we had not delayed, we could have come and gone twice by now.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, in Part I section I of his Undesigned Coincidences, notes that the short account of Jacob's refusal would suggest it was soon overcome, while Judah's words in Genesis 43:10 show it lasted as long as a journey to Egypt and back.

cites.quote: The simple account of Jacob's reluctance to part with Benjamin would lead us to suppose that it was expressed and overcome in a short time, and with no great effort. Yet we incidentally hear from Judah that this family struggle (for such it ... seems to have been) had occupied as much time as would have sufficed for a journey to Egypt
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

patterns.short: Jacob's dying words recall a sin told in one line
patterns.about: Reuben's sin with Bilhah is told in a single line that ends with Israel heard about it. Many years later Jacob's dying words to Reuben show how deeply the wrong had cut, and why Reuben lost his place as firstborn.

sides.label: Reuben's sin, briefly told
words: Reuben went in and slept with his father’s concubine Bilhah, and Israel heard about it.

sides.label: Jacob's dying words
words: because you went up to your father’s bed, onto my couch, and defiled it.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, in Part I section I of his Undesigned Coincidences, sets Jacob's words to Reuben in Genesis 49 beside the brief report in Genesis 35:22. Matthew Henry on Genesis 49:4 says the sin of forty years before is remembered against him, and Keil and Delitzsch on 49:4 name it as the sin of Genesis 35:22.

cites.quote: In the case of Reuben the allusion happens to be to a circumstance in his life with which we are already acquainted ... shows how deeply Jacob resented the wrong done him by this son many years before ... yet all that is reported of it in the Mosaic history is, and Israel heard it,
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: Jacob charges him particularly with the sin for which he was thus disgraced … It was forty years ago that he had been guilty of this sin, yet now it is remembered against him.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: His crime was, lying with Bilhah, his father's concubine ( Gen 35:22 ).
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Abraham pleads for the one city where Lot lives
patterns.about: Abraham pleads for Sodom again and again, down to ten righteous people, and the chapter never says why. An earlier chapter tells that his nephew Lot was living in Sodom.

sides.label: Abraham pleads for the city
words: Suppose ten are found there?

sides.label: Lot was living in Sodom
words: They also carried off Abram’s nephew Lot and his possessions, since Lot was living in Sodom.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, in Part I section II of his Undesigned Coincidences, argues that Abraham's earnest plea for Sodom alone, down to ten people, fits Lot's household living there (Genesis 14:12), though Genesis 18 never mentions Lot. Matthew Henry on Genesis 18 says Abraham prayed with an eye to Lot, as he had once rescued him by the sword.

cites.quote: our gathering from it a single hint that he had any relative within ten days' journey of the place ... And then we know, from what is elsewhere disclosed, that the family of Lot did actually dwell there at that time ... Surely, then, a coincidence between the zeal of the uncle and the danger of the brother's son is here detailed, though it is not expressed
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: He begins with a prayer that the righteous among them might be spared, and not involved in the common calamity, having an eye particularly to just Lot, whose disingenuous carriage towards him he had long since forgiven and forgotten, witness his friendly zeal to rescue him before by his sword and now by his prayers.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Isaac marries his cousin's daughter
patterns.about: Rebekah is the granddaughter of Abraham's brother Nahor, yet a fit match for Abraham's own son. That fits Sarah's long barrenness: Isaac came so late that he matched the next generation of Nahor's family.

sides.label: Rebekah, Nahor's granddaughter
words: I am the daughter of Bethuel, the son that Milcah bore to Nahor.

sides.label: Sarah was barren
words: But Sarai was barren; she had no children.

sides.label: Sarah past childbearing
words: Sarah had passed the age of childbearing.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, in Part I section III of his Undesigned Coincidences, notes that a granddaughter of Nahor is of age for Abraham's son, and that this fits what is said elsewhere of Sarah's long barrenness.

cites.quote: that a person of the third generation on Nahor's side is found of suitable years for one of the second generation on Abraham's side. Now what could harmonize more remarkably with a fact elsewhere asserted, though here not even touched upon, that Sarah, the wife of Abraham, was for a long time barren, and had no child till she was stricken in years ?
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

patterns.short: Rebekah's father is passed over again and again
patterns.about: Bethuel is alive, yet Rebekah runs to her mother's household, Laban greets the guest, the gifts go to brother and mother, and they ask her to stay. Years later Jacob asks for Laban by his grandfather's name.

sides.label: Rebekah runs to her mother
words: The girl ran and told her mother’s household about these things.
Now Rebekah had a brother named Laban, and he rushed out to the man at the spring.

sides.label: Bethuel is still alive
words: Laban and Bethuel answered, “This is from the LORD; we have no choice in the matter.

sides.label: Gifts and the delay
words: He also gave precious gifts to her brother and her mother.
But her brother and mother said, “Let the girl remain with us ten days or so.

sides.label: Jacob asks for Laban
words: “Do you know Laban the grandson of Nahor?” Jacob asked.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, in Part I section IV of his Undesigned Coincidences, traces how Bethuel is overlooked at each step of Genesis 24 and in Jacob's question in Genesis 29:5. Some commentators instead take Bethuel to have been dead.

cites.quote: The consistent insignificance of Bethuel in this whole affair. Yet he was alive, and, as the father of Rebekah, was likely, it might have been thought, to have been a conspicuous person in this contract of his daughter's marriage.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

patterns.short: Isaac's evening walk and his mother's death
patterns.about: Isaac goes out to the field in the evening, and the reason is not given. The chapter ends by saying he was comforted after his mother's death, and Sarah's death is told just before the servant set out.

sides.label: Sarah dies
words: She died in Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan, and Abraham went out to mourn and to weep for her.

sides.label: Isaac in the field
words: Early in the evening, Isaac went out to the field to meditate

sides.label: Isaac comforted
words: And Isaac loved her and was comforted after his mother’s death.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, in Part I section V of his Undesigned Coincidences, takes Isaac's evening meditation as grief for Sarah, and finds this borne out by the words that close Genesis 24.

cites.quote: But one of the last things that is recorded to have happened before the servant went to Haran, whence he was now returning, is the death and burial of Sarah ... What more likely than that her loss was the subject of Isaac's mournful meditation on this occasion ? But this conjecture is reduced almost to certainty by a few words incidentally dropped at the end of
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

patterns.short: Isaac blesses as if dying, then lives on for years
patterns.about: Isaac speaks as one near death, yet he is still alive when Jacob comes home many years later. The scene itself hints that he was ill: he must sit up to eat, trembles, and Esau expects to mourn him soon.

sides.label: Isaac expects to die
words: I am now old, and I do not know the day of my death.

sides.label: Signs he was ill
words: Please sit up and eat some of my game, so that you may bless me.

sides.label: Esau expects his death
words: The days of mourning for my father are at hand

sides.label: Isaac lives on
words: And Isaac lived 180 years.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, in Part I section VI of his Undesigned Coincidences, explains Isaac's long life after the blessing by a dangerous illness at the time, which he finds hinted in the details of Genesis 27.

cites.quote: that it was probably at a moment of dangerous sickness when he bethought himself of imparting the blessing — and I feel my conjecture supported by the following minute coincidences.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

patterns.short: Esau's threat waits on Isaac, who lives on for years
patterns.about: Esau puts off killing Jacob until his father has died. Isaac lives on many years, and when he dies, Esau and Jacob bury him together.

sides.label: Esau's threat
words: And Esau said in his heart, “The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then I will kill my brother Jacob.”

sides.label: The brothers bury Isaac
words: And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, in Part I section VI of his Undesigned Coincidences, links Esau's delay to Isaac's long life and to Esau's part in the burial. Matthew Henry on Genesis 27:41 says Esau put off the murder till his father died, and on Genesis 35:29 sets the burial beside that vow.

cites.quote: the prolongation of Isaac's life unexpectedly (as it should seem), may have had its influence in the continued protection of Jacob from Esau's anger ... we nevertheless find him anxious to do honour to his father's grave
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: Particular notice is taken of the amicable agreement of Esau and Jacob, in solemnizing their father's funeral ( Gen 35:29 ), to show how wonderfully God had changed Esau's mind since he vowed his brother's murder immediately after his father's death, Gen 27:41 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The foreign gods came with the Shechem captives
patterns.about: Jacob suddenly tells all who were with him to get rid of foreign gods. The chapter before tells how his sons carried off the women and children of Shechem, newly joined to his household.

sides.label: Put away the foreign gods
words: Get rid of the foreign gods that are among you.

sides.label: The captives of Shechem
words: They carried off all their possessions and women and children, and they plundered everything in their houses.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, in Part I section VII of his Undesigned Coincidences, explains the command by the captives of Shechem. Matthew Henry on Genesis 35:2 says the captives brought their gods with them, and Adam Clarke on the same verse thinks the images came very probably from the Shechemites.

cites.quote: These captives, then, so lately added to the company of Jacob, were in all probability the strangers alluded to, and the idols in their possession the gods of the strangers
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: The captives of Shechem brought their gods along with them, and perhaps Jacob's sons took some with the plunder.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: suppose that we allow, as is very probable, that their images and rings were got from strangers, the Syrians and the Shechemites
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Laban's welcome came after he saw the gold
patterns.about: Laban runs out to welcome the servant once he sees the ring and bracelets. The same man later cheats Jacob and changes his wages ten times.

sides.label: Laban sees the gifts
words: As soon as he saw the ring, and the bracelets on his sister’s wrists

sides.label: Laban's later dealings
words: and you have changed my wages ten times!

patterns.evidence: Blunt, in Part I section VIII of his Undesigned Coincidences, sees Laban's welcome as spurred by the gifts, of a piece with his later greed. Matthew Henry on Genesis 24:30 reads the welcome the same way from what the later story shows of Laban.

cites.quote: Hospitality was the virtue of his age and country ; in his case, however, it seems to have been no little stimulated by the sight of the ear-ring and the bracelets on his sister's hands, which the servant had already given
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: We know so much of Laban's character, by the following story, as to think that he would not have been so free of his entertainment if he had not hoped to be well paid for it
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Jacob's fear of men shows again and again
patterns.about: Across many years Jacob acts the same way: he slips away from Laban out of fear, splits his camp before Esau, fears the people of the land after Shechem, and frets that the brothers told of Benjamin.

sides.label: Fleeing Laban
words: “I was afraid,” Jacob answered, “for I thought you would take your daughters from me by force.

sides.label: Before Esau
words: In great fear and distress, Jacob divided his people into two camps

sides.label: After Shechem
words: We are few in number; if they unite against me and attack me, I and my household will be destroyed.”

sides.label: Over Benjamin
words: “Why did you bring this trouble upon me?” Israel asked.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, in Part I section VIII of his Undesigned Coincidences, gathers these scattered moments as one consistent trait in Jacob, drawn from life rather than designed.

cites.quote: Jacob should have learned, like maltreated animals, to have the fear of man habitually before his eyes. Now that it was so is evident from all the latter part of his history. ... I cannot persuade myself that these are not marks of a real character — especially when I consider that this identity is found in incidents spread over a period of a hundred years or more
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

patterns.short: Spices bound for a land that embalmed its dead
patterns.about: The traders who buy Joseph carry spices, balm, and myrrh to Egypt. Much later Joseph has his father embalmed, as the Egyptians did, so such goods would find a ready market there.

sides.label: Spices bound for Egypt
words: Their camels were carrying spices, balm, and myrrh on their way down to Egypt.

sides.label: Egypt embalms its dead
words: taking the forty days required to complete the embalming.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, in Part I section IX of his Undesigned Coincidences, sets the caravan's cargo beside the embalming of Jacob in Genesis 50:2-3. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown on Genesis 37:25 also say these goods were in great demand in Egypt for embalming.

cites.quote: is an incident which tallies remarkably well with what we read elsewhere, in a passage, however, having no reference whatever to the one in question. ... Hence, then, the camel-loads of spices which the Ishmaelites were bringing from Gilead, would naturally enough find an ample market in Egypt.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: For these articles there must have been an enormous demand in Egypt as they were constantly used in the process of embalming.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Egypt shown as a land of grain without saying so
patterns.about: Moses never says outright that Egypt grew much grain, yet it shows in passing: people went there in famine to buy grain, the Israelites gathered stubble all over Egypt, and the frogs got into ovens and kneading bowls.

sides.label: Abram goes to Egypt in famine
words: So Abram went down to Egypt to live there for a while because the famine was severe.

sides.label: All nations buy grain there
words: And every nation came to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain

sides.label: Stubble all over the land
words: So the people scattered all over the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.

sides.label: Frogs in ovens and bowls
words: into your ovens and kneading bowls

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section X: he finds many hints in the books of Moses that Egypt was a great grain country, such as the famines, the chief baker, the stubble and the kneading bowls, though it is never said in plain words.

cites.quote: I perceive in each and all of the following incidents, indirect indications of this one fact, that Egypt was already a great corn country, though I do not believe that such a fact is directly asserted in any passage in the whole Pentateuch.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

patterns.short: Why Egypt paid Pharaoh a fifth of its harvest
patterns.about: Joseph advised that a fifth of the harvest be taken in the good years. Chapters later, after the famine, he made it a lasting law that a fifth of the produce belongs to Pharaoh: the same share, now kept for good.

sides.label: A fifth taken in the good years
words: to take a fifth of the harvest of Egypt during the seven years of abundance.

sides.label: A fifth made a lasting law
words: So Joseph established a law that a fifth of the produce belongs to Pharaoh

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XI: the fifth that Joseph made law after the famine is the same share he had taken up before it, a short-term measure made lasting.

cites.quote: Now this was, as we have been told in a former chapter, precisely the proportion which Joseph had "taken up" before the famine began.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

patterns.short: Why Joseph left the priests their land
patterns.about: When Joseph bought up all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, he did not take the priests' land. Earlier Pharaoh had given Joseph a priest's daughter as his wife, so the priests stood high with both Pharaoh and Joseph.

sides.label: The priests keep their land
words: However, he did not acquire the priests’ portion of the land

sides.label: Joseph marries a priest's daughter
words: and he gave him Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, to be his wife.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XI: since Pharaoh honoured the priests and Joseph had married a priest's daughter, it was natural that their lands were spared.

cites.quote: When, therefore, the priests were thus held in esteem by Pharaoh, and when the minister of Pharaoh, under whose immediate directions all the regulations of the polity of Egypt were at that time conducted, had the daughter of one of them for his wife, is it not the most natural thing in the world to have happened, that their lands should be spared ?
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

patterns.short: Joseph's love for his father shows at every turn
patterns.about: Each time Joseph meets his brothers he asks if his father is alive. He gives way when Judah speaks of what losing the boy would do to their father, his first words then are about his father, and after Jacob dies the brothers plead in their father's name.

sides.label: Joseph asks after his father
words: How is your elderly father you told me about? Is he still alive?

sides.label: Judah pleads for the father
words: he will die.

sides.label: His first words
words: Is my father still alive?

sides.label: The brothers plead in his name
words: Before he died, your father commanded,

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XII: Joseph's love for his father runs through his whole story, in his questions, in what moves him to make himself known, and in how his brothers appeal to him.

cites.quote: There is one quality ... which runs like a thread through his whole history — his affection for his father.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

patterns.short: How Amram could marry his father's sister
patterns.about: Exodus says Amram, Levi's grandson, married his father's sister Jochebed, which seems to cross a generation. Numbers adds in passing that she was born to Levi in Egypt, long after Kohath, who came down from Canaan with Jacob.

sides.label: Amram marries his aunt
words: The sons of Kohath were Amram
And Amram married his father’s sister Jochebed

sides.label: Kohath comes down to Egypt
words: The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.

sides.label: Jochebed born in Egypt
words: born to Levi in Egypt.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XIII: the passing note in Numbers that Jochebed was born in Egypt makes her much younger than her brother Kohath, born in Canaan, and so about the age of his son Amram.

cites.quote: From this we may conclude, that Jochebed was born to Levi long after his other children ; that Kohath, her brother , who was born in Canaan, was much older than herself ... Amram of the second descent would be about coeval with Jochebed of the first.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

patterns.short: Why priests were told not to drink wine just then
patterns.about: Nadab and Abihu offered fire the LORD had not commanded and died. Soon after, with no reason given, Aaron and his sons are forbidden wine when they go into the Tent of Meeting. The law fits the rash act it follows.

sides.label: Unauthorized fire
words: offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, contrary to His command.

sides.label: No wine at the Tent
words: You and your sons are not to drink wine or strong drink when you enter the Tent of Meeting

patterns.limit: The text does not say they had been drinking.
patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XIV; Henry, Keil and Delitzsch, and Barnes on Leviticus 10: each ties the law against wine for priests on duty to the sin of Nadab and Abihu just before it.

cites.quote: I conclude, therefore, that there was a relation (though it is not asserted) between the specific offence and the general law ; the more so, because the sin against which that law is directed is just of a kind to have produced the rash and inconsiderate act of which Aaron's sons were guilty.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: There is reason to suspect that they were drunk when they did it, because of the law which was given upon this occasion
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The motive for laying down on this particular occasion a prohibition which was to hold good for all time, seems to lie in the event recorded in Lev 10:1
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: When the priest was on duty he was to abstain from wine and strong drink, lest he should commit excess (see Lev 10:1 ), and so become disqualified for carrying out the precepts of the ceremonial Law.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Who the men unclean from a dead body may have been
patterns.about: At the first Passover in the wilderness some men were unclean from a dead body. Six days before, Aaron's two cousins had carried out the bodies of Nadab and Abihu. The men counted just before and just after number the same, so none of them seems to have died in between.

sides.label: Bodies carried out of the camp
words: Moses summoned Mishael and Elzaphan

sides.label: Men unclean at the Passover
words: But there were some men who were unclean due to a dead body

sides.label: The count before
words: a total of 603,550 men.

sides.label: The count after
words: And all those counted totaled 603,550.

patterns.limit: A likely reading; the text does not name the men.
patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XV, and Barnes on Numbers 9:6: both suggest the men were Mishael and Elzaphan, who carried out the bodies of Nadab and Abihu shortly before this Passover.

cites.quote: My conclusion, therefore, is that these " certain men," who were defiled, were no others than Mishael and Elzaphan, who had carried out the dead bodies of Nadab and Abihu.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: Probably Mishael and Elizaphan, who buried their cousins, Nadab and Abihu, within a week of this Passover
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Why Amalek attacked at Rephidim
patterns.about: Water came from the rock at Rephidim, and then Amalek attacked Israel at the same place. In that dry land wells were fought over, so the new water may be what drew the attack. Later Israel is told Amalek had no fear of God.

sides.label: Water from the rock
words: And when you strike the rock, water will come out of it for the people to drink.

sides.label: Amalek attacks there
words: After this, the Amalekites came and attacked the Israelites at Rephidim.

sides.label: No fear of God
words: they had no fear of God.

patterns.limit: The text does not say why Amalek attacked.
patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XVI: in a land where wells were often fought over, the water given at Rephidim and Amalek's attack at the same place fit together, though the text links them only by time.

cites.quote: the sudden gushing of the water from the rock (which was the sudden discovery of an invaluable treasure), and the subsequent onset of the Amalekites at the very same place ... do coincide very remarkably with one another
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

patterns.short: Barley ripe, wheat not, at the time of the hail
patterns.about: The hail fell shortly before the Passover and struck the barley, already ripe, but not the wheat. The feasts agree: a sheaf is waved at the Passover, and loaves of new grain come only seven weeks later, so barley ripened weeks before wheat.

sides.label: Hail strikes the barley
words: since the barley was ripe
but the wheat and spelt were not destroyed, because they are late crops.)

sides.label: The first sheaf
words: you are to bring to the priest a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest.

sides.label: New grain seven weeks later
words: you are to count off seven full weeks.

sides.label: Barley harvest, then wheat
words: until the barley and wheat harvests were finished.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XVII: the feasts show barley ripe at the Passover and wheat seven weeks later, and the hail, near the Passover, struck the barley but not the wheat.

cites.quote: In a word then, my argument is this — that at the Passover the barley in Judea was ripe, but that the wheat was not, seven weeks having yet to elapse before the first-fruits of the loaves could be offered. ... The two statements on being compared together, agree together.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

patterns.short: Why Merari got twice the carts of Gershon
patterns.about: Moses gave the Gershonites two carts and the Merarites four, with no reason given. An earlier chapter lists their loads: Gershon carried the curtains and coverings, Merari the frames, crossbars, posts and bases.

sides.label: Two carts and four carts
words: He gave the Gershonites two carts and four oxen
and he gave the Merarites four carts and eight oxen

sides.label: Gershon carries the curtains
words: They are to carry the curtains of the tabernacle

sides.label: Merari carries the frames
words: to carry the frames of the tabernacle with its crossbars, posts, and bases

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XVIII; Henry, Keil and Delitzsch, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Clarke and Barnes on Numbers 7: each explains the extra carts by the heavier loads Numbers 4 gives the Merarites.

cites.quote: And hence it is easy to see why more oxen and waggons were assigned to the one family than to the other.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: The Gershonites, that had the light carriage, the curtains and hangings, had but two wagons, and two yoke of oxen ... The Merarites, that had the heavy carriage, and that which was most unwieldy, the boards, pillars, sockets, etc., had four wagons
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He gave two waggons and four oxen to the Gershonites, and four waggons and eight oxen to the Merarites, as the former had less weight to carry, in the coverings and curtains of the dwelling and the hangings of the court, than the latter, who had to take charge of the beams and pillars
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The Merarites had twice the number of wagons and oxen appropriated to them that the Gershonites had, obviously because, while the latter had charge only of the coverings and hangings ... the former were appointed to transport all the heavy and bulky materials
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Because they had the boards, bars, pillars, and sockets of the tabernacle to carry ... therefore they had as many more wagons as the Gershonites.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: To the Gershonites, who had to transport the hangings and coverings of the tabernacle, two wagons are assigned: to the Merarites, who had the charge of the solid parts of the tabernacle, four wagons.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Judah leads the march, as the camp plan implies
patterns.about: Judah camps on the east, and the first trumpet blast moves the camps on the east. So when Israel leaves Sinai, Judah should go first, and the account of the march says it did.

sides.label: Judah camps on the east
words: On the east side, toward the sunrise, the divisions of Judah are to camp under their standard:

sides.label: First blast moves the east
words: When you sound short blasts, the camps that lie on the east side are to set out.

sides.label: Judah sets out first
words: First, the divisions of the camp of Judah set out under their standard

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XIX, joins the east camp of Judah and the first blast to show Judah should lead, as it does. Keil and Delitzsch, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Clarke on Numbers 10:5-6 each tie the blasts to the camp order.

cites.quote: Thus it is implied from two passages brought together from two chapters, separated by the intervention of eight others relating to things indifferent, that Judah was to lead in any march. Now we see in the account of a specific movement of the camp from Sinai, with which I introduced these remarks, that on that occasion Judah did in fact lead.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: At the first blast the tribes on the east, i.e., those who were encamped in the front of the tabernacle, were to break up; at the second, those who were encamped on the south; and so on in the order prescribed in ch. 2
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: One alarm was the recognized signal for the eastern division of the camp (the tribes of Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun) to march; two alarms gave the signal for the southern to move
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: A single alarm, as above stated, was a signal for the eastward division to march ... the east and south camps alone are mentioned; the first containing Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Reuben moves second, as the camp plan implies
patterns.about: Reuben camps on the south, and the second trumpet blast moves the camps on the south. So Reuben should be the second camp to leave Sinai, and the account of the march says it was.

sides.label: Reuben camps on the south
words: On the south side, the divisions of Reuben are to camp under their standard:

sides.label: Second blast moves the south
words: When you sound the short blasts a second time, the camps that lie on the south side are to set out.

sides.label: Reuben sets out next
words: Then the divisions of the camp of Reuben set out under their standard

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XIX, joins the south camp of Reuben and the second blast to show Reuben should move second, as it does. Keil and Delitzsch, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Clarke on Numbers 10:5-6 tie the second blast to the south camp.

cites.quote: the passage last quoted (which is far removed from this) informs us that Reuben was on the south side of the Tabernacle ; the camp of Reuben therefore it was, which was appointed to move when the alarm was blown the second time.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: At the first blast the tribes on the east, i.e., those who were encamped in the front of the tabernacle, were to break up; at the second, those who were encamped on the south; and so on in the order prescribed in ch. 2
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: One alarm was the recognized signal for the eastern division of the camp (the tribes of Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun) to march; two alarms gave the signal for the southern to move
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The camps, or grand divisions of this great army, always lay, as we have already seen, to the east, south, west, and north: and here the east and south camps alone are mentioned; the first containing Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun; the second, Reuben, Simeon, and Gad.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The rebels camped on the same side of the tabernacle
patterns.about: Korah, of the clan of Kohath, joins with men of Reuben against Moses. Chapters earlier we are told in passing that the Kohathites camped on the south side, and so did Reuben. The plotters were neighbours.

sides.label: Korah and Reubenites rebel
words: Now Korah son of Izhar, the son of Kohath son of Levi, along with some Reubenites

sides.label: Kohath camps on the south
words: The clans of the Kohathites were to camp on the south side of the tabernacle,

sides.label: Reuben camps on the south
words: On the south side, the divisions of Reuben are to camp under their standard:

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XX, notes that Kohath and Reuben camped on the same side. Barnes, Matthew Henry and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Numbers 16:1 each say the shared south side gave the plotters easy contact.

cites.quote: The family of Kohath, therefore, and the family of Reuben, both pitched on the same side of the Tabernacle — they were neighbours, and were therefore conveniently situated for taking secret counsel together.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: The Reubenites encamped near to the Kohathites (compare Num 2:25 and plan), and thus the two families were conveniently situated for taking counsel together.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The Kohathites encamped on the same side of the tabernacle that the Reubenites did, which perhaps gave Korah an opportunity of drawing them in
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: These malcontents had been incited by the artful representations of Korah ( Jde 1:11 ), with whom the position of their camp on the south side afforded them facilities of frequent intercourse.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Korah's sons are not named at the doomed tents
patterns.about: At the judgment only the families of Dathan and Abiram are said to stand at their tents. Ten chapters later we learn in passing that the line of Korah did not die out. The first account quietly allows for the second.

sides.label: Only two families at the tents
words: Meanwhile, Dathan and Abiram had come out and stood at the entrances to their tents with their wives and children and infants.

sides.label: Korah's line survives
words: However, the line of Korah did not die out.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XX, notes that the sons of Dathan and Abiram are named at the tents but not those of Korah. Clarke on Numbers 26:11 makes the same reading of Numbers 16:27.

cites.quote: Here we perceive that mention is made of the sons of Dathan and the sons of Abiram, but not of the sons of Korah.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: on a close inspection of Num 16:27 , we shall find that the sons and the little ones of Dathan and Abiram alone are mentioned. ... Here is no mention of the children of Korah, they therefore escaped
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Reuben and Gad ask together, as camp neighbours
patterns.about: Reuben and Gad together ask for land east of the Jordan. Earlier we were told that Gad camped in Reuben's division on the south side, so the two tribes had long lived and marched side by side.

sides.label: Reuben and Gad ask for Gilead
words: Now the Reubenites and Gadites, who had very large herds and flocks

sides.label: Gad camps with Reuben
words: On the south side, the divisions of Reuben are to camp under their standard:
Next will be the tribe of Gad.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XXI, links the joint request to Gad being part of Reuben's camp. Matthew Henry on Numbers 32:1-5 says the two tribes camped under one standard and so could settle the matter together.

cites.quote: For I read in the 2nd chapter of Numbers (v. 10, 14), that the camp of Reuben was on the south side of the Tabernacle , and that the tribe of Gad formed a division of the camp of Reuben.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: Reuben and Gad were encamped under the same standard, and so had the better opportunity of comparing notes, and settling this matter between themselves.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Hobab's answer comes out later, in Judges
patterns.about: Moses begs Hobab to come with Israel, and we are never told what he decided. Long after, Judges mentions in passing that the family of Moses' father-in-law, the Kenite, went up with Judah. So the invitation was taken up.

sides.label: Moses invites Hobab
words: “I will not go,” Hobab replied.
“Please do not leave us,” Moses said

sides.label: The Kenites go up with Judah
words: Now the descendants of Moses’ father-in-law, the Kenite, went up with the men of Judah

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XXII, says Judges shows the invitation was accepted. Keil and Delitzsch, Matthew Henry, Clarke and Barnes on Numbers 10:29-32 each draw the same conclusion from Judges 1:16.

cites.quote: Thus we learn, for the first time, that Moses' invitation to his father-in-law was accepted — that he joined himself to the Israelites, and shared their fortunes.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: This is raised to a certainty by the fact that, at the commencement of the period of the Judges, the sons of the brother-in-law of Moses went into the desert of Judah to the south of Arad along with the sons of Judah ( Jdg 1:16 ), and therefore had entered Canaan with the Israelites
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: We do not find any reply that Hobab here made to Moses, and therefore we hope that his silence gave consent, and he did not leave them ... And we find ( Jdg 1:16 ; Sa1 15:6 ) that his family was no loser by it.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: From the strong expostulations in Num 10:31 and Num 10:32 , and from Jdg 1:16 ; Jdg 4:11 , and Sa1 15:6 , it is likely that Hobab changed his mind; or that, if he did go back to Midian, he returned again to Israel, as the above scriptures show that his posterity dwelt among the Israelites in Canaan.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Hobab Jdg 1:16 ; Jdg 4:11 eventually accompanied the Israelites and obtained a settlement with them in the land of Canaan.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: News travels far in these early books
patterns.about: A king of Moab knows of a seer by the Euphrates. Abraham hears of Nahor's children far away, Jethro hears all God did for Israel, and Moses tells Edom it already knows Israel's hardship. The books assume news moved freely, without explaining it.

sides.label: Balak sends to Pethor
words: he sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor at Pethor, which is by the Euphrates

sides.label: Abraham hears of Nahor's sons
words: Some time later, Abraham was told, “Milcah has also borne sons to your brother Nahor:

sides.label: Jethro hears the news
words: heard about all that God had done for Moses and His people Israel

sides.label: Edom already knows
words: You know all the hardship that has befallen us,

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, sections XXIII and XXIV, gathers many passages in the books of Moses that take for granted that news passed freely among the desert peoples, and counts this quiet agreement a sign of truth.

cites.quote: Now all these unconnected matters hint at this one circumstance., that intelligence travelled through the tribes of the Desert more freely and rapidly than might have been thought ... the consistency with which the writings of Moses imply such a fact (for they neither affirm it, nor trouble themselves about explaining it) is a feature of truth in those writings
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

patterns.short: Balaam heads home but dies among the Midianites
patterns.about: Elders of both Moab and Midian fetch Balaam. After Moab, Midian drops out of the story, and Balaam sets off for home. Much later he is found slain among the Midianites, the other people who had sent for him.

sides.label: Moab and Midian send for him
words: The elders of Moab and Midian departed with the fees for divination in hand.

sides.label: Balaam sets off home
words: Then Balaam arose and returned to his homeland

sides.label: Slain with Midian's kings
words: They also killed Balaam son of Beor with the sword.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XXIV: the joint embassy from Moab and Midian explains why Balaam, sent away from Moab, is later found dead among the Midianites.

cites.quote: The undesigned coincidence lies in the elders of Moab and the elders of Midian going to Balaam ; in Midian being then mentioned no more, till Balaam, having been sent away from Moab, apparently that he might go home, is subsequently found a corpse amongst the slaughtered Midianites.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

patterns.short: Simeon shrinks, and the named sinner was a Simeonite
patterns.about: The one man named in the sin at Peor is a leader of Simeon. In the next count Simeon has fallen from 59,300 to 22,200, far more than any other tribe, though no reason is given. The plague seems to have struck Simeon hardest.

sides.label: Zimri a Simeonite leader
words: was Zimri son of Salu, the leader of a Simeonite family.

sides.label: Simeon at Sinai
words: those registered to the tribe of Simeon numbered 59,300.

sides.label: Simeon on the plains of Moab
words: These were the clans of Simeon, and there were 22,200 men.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XXV, links Simeon's loss to the plague and to Zimri. Barnes on the census in Numbers 26 and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Numbers 26:12 make the same link.

cites.quote: Yet it does seem very natural to think, that, in the recent Plague, the tribe to which Zimri belonged, who is mentioned as a leading person in it with great emphasis, was the tribe upon which the chief fury of the scourge fell
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: The most remarkable decrease is in Simeon, which now shows less than half its former strength. To this tribe Zimri, the chief offender in the recent transgression, belonged Num 25:14 . Probably his tribesmen generally had followed his example, and had accordingly suffered most severely in the plague.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: It is supposed that this tribe had been pre-eminent in the guilt of Baal-peor and had consequently been greatly reduced in numbers.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Moses blesses every tribe but Simeon
patterns.about: Moses' last blessing goes from Reuben straight to Judah and never names Simeon, the tribe of Zimri. Later Simeon's land is only a share taken out of Judah's. Both fit a tribe in disgrace after Peor.

sides.label: Zimri a Simeonite leader
words: was Zimri son of Salu, the leader of a Simeonite family.

sides.label: Reuben, then Judah
words: Let Reuben live and not die, nor his men be few.”
And concerning Judah he said:

sides.label: Simeon's land inside Judah
words: The inheritance of the Simeonites was taken from the territory of Judah

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XXV, ties the missing blessing and Simeon's small share inside Judah to the sin at Peor. Barnes on Deuteronomy 33:6 links the omission to new sins, the tribe's shrinking and its land within Judah.

cites.quote: the tribe of Simeon he passes over in silence, and none but the tribe of Simeon ... which does in fact, as I apprehend, point to this same matter of Baal-Peor.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: the little consideration paid to this tribe by their brethren shortly afterwards, in the allotment of the portions of the Holy Land, implies it to have been in disgrace — their inheritance being only the remnant of that assigned to the children of Judah
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: Rather had this latter tribe added new sins to those which Jacob denounced (compare Num 26:5 note). Accordingly, though very numerous at the Exodus, it had surprisingly diminished before the death of Moses (compare Num 1:22-23 with Num 26:12-14 ); and eventually it found territory adequate for its wants within the limits of another tribe, Judah.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: For centuries Israel rides donkeys, not horses
patterns.about: The law tells a future king not to gather many horses. For centuries after, Israel's leaders ride donkeys, Kish loses donkeys, and even Absalom rides a mule. Horses are missing just where we might expect them.

sides.label: No many horses for the king
words: But the king must not acquire many horses for himself

sides.label: Leaders ride white donkeys
words: You who ride white donkeys

sides.label: Kish's donkeys are lost
words: One day the donkeys of Saul’s father Kish wandered off

sides.label: Absalom on a mule
words: Now Absalom was riding on his mule

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XXVI, sets the law against many horses beside the many passages where Israel rides donkeys and mules. Matthew Henry on Deuteronomy 17:16 notes that donkeys and mules were in common use and that the judges rode donkeys.

cites.quote: the injunction in Deuteronomy forbidding the multiplication of horses ... when compared with the various ways — many of them very indirect — in which it transpires incidentally in the History of the Israelites for several centuries, that no horses were forthcoming where their presence was to be expected, furnishes a coincidence very significant of truth
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: He that rode upon a horse (a stately creature) in a country where asses and mules were generally used looked very great; ... (when God was their King, his judges rode on asses, Jdg 5:10 ; Jdg 12:14 )
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Horses in these years belong to Israel's enemies
patterns.about: After the law against many horses, the horses and chariots in Judges and Samuel belong to Israel's foes, such as Sisera's stallions and the chariots of the king of Zobah. At one great defeat, Israel's dead are all foot soldiers.

sides.label: No many horses for the king
words: But the king must not acquire many horses for himself

sides.label: The enemy's stallions
words: Then the hooves of horses thundered

sides.label: Israel's foot soldiers fall
words: thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell.

sides.label: Chariots taken from Zobah's king
words: David captured from him a thousand chariots
he hamstrung all the horses except a hundred he kept for the chariots.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences, Part I, section XXVI, notes that horses in this period belong to those who were not Israelites. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on 2 Samuel 8:4 says David lamed the horses because they were forbidden to Israel, while its neighbours relied on cavalry.

cites.quote: Wherever horses and horsemen are mentioned during this period of the Jewish history, it is in reference to those who were not Israelites.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: The horses were thus mutilated because they were forbidden to the Hebrews, both in war and agriculture. So it was of no use to keep them. Besides, their neighbors placed much dependence on cavalry
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Flax drying on the roof fits the time of the crossing
patterns.about: Rahab hid the spies under stalks of flax laid out on her roof. The crossing came days later, at harvest, in the first month, and Exodus shows flax and barley coming on together. Freshly cut flax on the roof fits that very season.

sides.label: Spies hidden under flax
words: hidden them among the stalks of flax that she had laid out there.

sides.label: Jordan full at harvest
words: Now the Jordan overflows its banks throughout the harvest season.

sides.label: Crossed in the first month
words: On the tenth day of the first month the people went up from the Jordan

sides.label: Flax and barley together
words: the barley was ripe and the flax was in bloom;

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences Part II section I, ties Rahab's flax stalks to the barley harvest at which Israel crossed. Adam Clarke, on Joshua 2:6, says the season was when flax is ripe, so her flax was likely newly pulled and drying.

cites.quote: Is it possible for the most jealous examiner of human testimony to imagine that these flax-stalks were fixed upon above all things in the world for the covering of the spies, because they were known to be ripe with the barley, and the barley was known to be ripe at the Passover, and the Passover was known to be the season when the Israelites set foot in Canaan?
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: as this was about the season, viz., the end of March or the beginning of April, in which the flax is ripe in that country, consequently Rahab's flax might have been recently pulled, and was now drying on the roof of her house.

patterns.short: Only Lachish held out to a second day

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences Part II section II, reads the second day as a hint that Lachish was strong, borne out by Kings and Jeremiah. patterns.short: David's last charge passes over Jonathan's son
patterns.about: Dying, David commends Barzillai's sons but says nothing of Mephibosheth, whom he had sworn to treat kindly. Ziba had said Mephibosheth hoped for the throne, David split the land between them, and later spared him only for the oath. David may have stayed unsure of him.

words: ‘Today, the house of Israel will restore to me the kingdom of my grandfather.’

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences Part II section XVI, explains David's silence about Mephibosheth on his deathbed by his doubt of Mephibosheth's loyalty in Absalom's revolt. Most commentators instead take Ziba's report as slander.

cites.quote: is it not rather a most natural and veracious coincidence, that David, in commending on his death-bed some of his stanch and trustworthy friends to Solomon his son, should have omitted all mention of Mephibosheth, dissatisfied as he was, and ever had been, with his explanations of very suspicious conduct, at a very critical hour ?

patterns.about: The Tent of Meeting stood at Shiloh, which another book places between Bethel and Shechem, in Ephraim. Ephraim then speaks to Gideon and to Jephthah as if no war should be fought without it. Holding the place of worship fits that leading, haughty tone.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences Part II section XVII, finds Ephraim the leading tribe, chiefly because the Tabernacle stood at Shiloh within it, and sees that rank in its angry words to Gideon and Jephthah. Joshua does not say where Shiloh was; it must be inferred.

cites.quote: The comparative importance of Ephraim amongst the tribes during the time of the Judges is further detected in the tone of authority, not to say menace, which it occasionally assumes towards its weaker brethren.

patterns.short: Jerusalem on the line of Judah and Benjamin binds them
patterns.about: One passage places Jerusalem among the people of Judah, and Benjamin's list of towns includes it, so the city stood on the border of both. When the kingdom split, Benjamin stayed with Judah. Sharing the city and its temple fits that bond.

sides.label: Jerusalem in Benjamin's list
words: Jebus (that is, Jerusalem),
This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Benjamin.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences Part II section XVII, notes one text puts Jerusalem in Judah and another in Benjamin, so the Temple rose on the border of both, binding them. Barnes on 1 Kings 12:21 explains Benjamin's loyalty to Judah by the shared capital on their border.

cites.quote: I look again, and learn that a temple was built for national worship in a city, which one text places in Judah, and a parallel text in Benjamin, leaving me to infer (as was the fact) that the city was on the confines of both, and that upon the confines of both (as was also the fact) the foundations of the Temple were laid.

patterns.short: Jeroboam ran the labor gangs that later broke away
patterns.about: Solomon put the Ephraimite Jeroboam over the forced labor of the house of Joseph. When Solomon dies, the tribes complain of a heavy yoke, stone the man over the forced labor, and make Jeroboam king. His post fits the revolt that followed.

words: “Your father put a heavy yoke on us.

sides.label: The labor chief stoned

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences Part II section XVII, says Jeroboam's charge over Ephraim's labor gave him the means to build his revolt, and notes the people stoned the very officer of the levy. Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke, on 1 Kings 11:28, both trace the revolt to that heavy work, which Jeroboam turned to his use.

cites.quote: we have an Ephraimite, even Jeroboam, with every talent for mischief, endowed with every opportunity for exercising it, put into an office which at once invested him with authority, and secured him from suspicion, so that his future crown was but the consummation of his present intrigues
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: According to Kg1 12:4 , the reason for the rebellion is to be sought for in the appointment of the Ephraimites to heavy works. This awakened afresh the old antipathy of that tribe to Judah, and Jeroboam availed himself of this to instigate a rebellion.

patterns.short: Dan already had its own image and priests
patterns.about: Jeroboam set one calf at Dan. Long before, the Danites had set up Micah's carved image there with their own priests, all the time the house of God was at Shiloh. A town used to worship apart from the house of God suited his plan.

sides.label: Micah's image at Dan

So they set up for themselves Micah’s graven image,

sides.label: A calf set up in Dan
words: One calf he set up in Bethel, and the other in Dan.

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences Part II section XVII, finds Jeroboam's reason for Dan in the image worship set up there by the Danites. Henry on 1 Kings 12:29 gives Micah's images as one reason, and Keil and Delitzsch on 1 Kings 12:28-29 say Dan was already a place of worship from that image.

cites.quote: I discover a very sufficient reason for his choice of Dan for the other, exclusive of all consideration of local convenience, — the curious circumstance, that in this town there had already prevailed for ages a form of worship, or of idolatry (I should rather say), very closely resembling that which he now proposed to set up throughout Israel

patterns.short: Golden calves from a man back from Egypt
patterns.about: Jeroboam fled to Egypt and stayed there until Solomon died. Back home, he made two golden calves for the people to worship. The text never links the two, but his years in Egypt fit his choice of a calf.

sides.label: Jeroboam in Egypt
words: But Jeroboam arose and fled to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, where he remained until the death of Solomon.

sides.label: Two golden calves
words: the king made two golden calves

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences Part II section XVII, says Jeroboam's stay in Egypt and the choice of a calf corroborate each other, though no hint links them. Henry on 1 Kings 12:28 thinks he more probably took up the worship of the Egyptians, among whom he had stayed.

cites.quote: no hint, the most remote, is thrown out, that his sojourn in that idolatrous land, and the peculiar nature of its idolatry, influenced him in the choice of a calf for the representative of his own God, though the one fact does very curiously corroborate the other

patterns.short: An old quarrel over the king comes back at the split
patterns.about: Bringing David home, Israel claims ten shares in the king and Judah claims him as kin, and Judah's words are the harsher. When the kingdom breaks under Rehoboam, Israel cries, what portion do we have in David. The breach had been opening for a long time.

sides.label: Ten shares in the king
words: “We did this because the king is our relative.
“We have ten shares in the king,” answered the men of Israel,

sides.label: No portion in David
words: “What portion do we have in David, and what inheritance in the son of Jesse?

patterns.evidence: Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences Part II section XVII, sees in the quarrel over David's return a breach already widening toward the split. Keil and Delitzsch, opening 1 Kings 12, say the old jealousy of Ephraim and Judah, which broke out at that quarrel, issued in the division of the kingdom.

cites.quote: the fierce words that passed between the men of Israel and the men of Judah, on the subject of the restoration of David to the throne, the former claiming ten parts in him, the latter nearness of ... still indicate that the breach was gradually widening, and that, however sudden was the final disruption of the bond of union, events had weakened it long before.
cites.read: the 1863 text in the CC0 transcription at github.com/nick-lang/undesigned-coincidences-paley-blunt (commit c529753)

cites.quote: The jealousy which had prevailed from time immemorial between Ephraim and Judah, the two most powerful tribes of the covenant nation, and had broken out on different occasions into open hostilities ( Jdg 8:1 .; Sa2 2:9 ; Sa2 19:42 .), issued, on the death of Solomon, in the division of the kingdom

patterns.short: Israel walls Ramah as its faithful leave for Judah
patterns.about: The stronger king of Israel fortifies Ramah to stop anyone going to Asa, and weaker Judah tears it down rather than keep it. Another book explains why. Levites and all who sought the LORD were leaving Israel for Jerusalem.

Henry on 1 Kings 15 says Ramah was meant to stop those who would come to worship, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on 1 Kings 15:17 say Baasha feared his subjects would leave.

cites.quote: Here I find a coincidence of the most satisfactory kind, between the building of Ramah by Israel., the overthrow of it by Judah, and the tide of emigration which was setting in from Israel towards Judah, by reason of Jeroboam's idolatry.

patterns.short: Judah's armies swell after the faithful come south
patterns.about: The faithful of Israel moved to Judah and strengthened it. Judah's army counts then rise from 180,000 under Rehoboam to 400,000 under Abijah and 580,000 under Asa, though no verse links the numbers to the move.

cites.quote: Still keeping in mind this single consideration, that the more godly of the people of the ten tribes were disgusted at the calves, and retired, we may at once account for the progressive augmentation of the armies of Judah, and the corresponding decrease of the armies of Israel, which the subsequent history of the two kingdoms casually, and at intervals, displays.

cites.quote: On the other hand, we may trace (the act, it must be observed, is altogether our own, no such comparison being instituted in the history,) the gradual decay and depopulation of the kingdom of Israel.

patterns.short: Jeroboam rules from the tribes' old meeting place

sides.label: Jeroboam lives at Shechem
words: Then Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there.

while he himself traveled on a day’s journey into the wilderness.

words: For he married a daughter of Ahab
