patterns.short: Do not be called Rabbi, father or instructor
patterns.about: Against the scribes' love of titles, Jesus tells His disciples not to be called Rabbi, not to call anyone on earth father, and not to be called instructors, for they have one Teacher, one Father and one Instructor.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Matthew 23:8 to 10, says the charge not to be called Rabbi or master is repeated twice.

cites.quote: It is repeated twice; Be not called Rabbi, neither be ye called Master or Guide
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees
patterns.about: Jesus pronounces woe on the scribes and Pharisees again and again, each time naming a fault. The old count is eight, with verse 14, which some copies have; the BSB text has seven.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Matthew 23:13, counts eight woes against the scribes and Pharisees, set against the eight blessings of chapter 5. Adam Clarke, at the end of the chapter, also says the Lord pronounces eight woes in verses 13 to 39.

cites.quote: In these verses we have eight woes levelled directly against the scribes and Pharisees by our Lord Jesus Christ, like so many claps of thunder, or flashes of lightning, from mount Sinai.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: From the 13th to the 39th verse, our Lord pronounces eight woes, or rather pathetic declarations, against the scribes and Pharisees.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: See to it that no one deceives you
patterns.about: Jesus begins His answer about the end with a warning against being deceived, and comes back to it: many will come in His name, false prophets will mislead many, and false Christs would deceive even the elect.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Matthew 24:23 to 26, speaks of the repeated caution to take heed of being ensnared by false Christs and false prophets.

cites.quote: And now comes in the repeated caution, which was opened before, to take heed of being ensnared by false Christs, and false prophets
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Keep watch, for you do not know the day
patterns.about: After the sayings about the coming of the Son of Man, Jesus says keep watch, for you do not know the day. After the parable of the ten virgins He says it again in nearly the same words.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Matthew 25:13, notes that the charge to watch was given before at 24:42 and is repeated here as the most needful caution.

cites.quote: Watch therefore, We had it before ( Mat 24:42 ), and here it is repeated as the most needful caution.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The Passover, named again and again
patterns.about: The chapter of the betrayal is set at the Passover. Jesus names it two days ahead, the disciples ask where to prepare it, and they prepare it as He directed before the supper.
patterns.evidence: Adam Clarke, on Matthew 26:26, notes that the Lord and His disciples call the lamb the Passover several times in this chapter.

cites.quote: our Lord and his disciples call this lamb the passover, several times in this chapter
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Go to Galilee; there you will see Him
patterns.about: The angel tells the women that Jesus is going ahead of them into Galilee, Jesus Himself says the same, and the chapter ends with the eleven on the mountain in Galilee, as He had promised before His death.
patterns.evidence: David Brown, in Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Matthew 28:16, says the promise given before the resurrection and twice repeated after it explains the great gathering in Galilee.

cites.quote: the promise before His resurrection, twice repeated after it, best explains this immense gathering
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Immediately, a word Mark uses more than anyone
patterns.about: The word given as immediately, at once or as soon as comes more than thirty times in Mark, more often than in any other book of the New Testament, and most of them in the early chapters.
patterns.evidence: Adam Clarke, on Mark 1:28, says the word for immediately occurs more often in Mark than in any other writer of the New Testament.

cites.quote: The word, ευθεως, immediately, occurs more frequently in this evangelist than in any other writer of the new covenant
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: He who has ears to hear, let him hear
patterns.about: Jesus begins the parable of the sower with listen and ends it with he who has ears to hear, let him hear. He says it again later and adds pay attention to what you hear. The soils are people who hear the word.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Mark 4, notes the parable begins with hearken and ends with ears to hear, and that at verse 23 the Lord says it again. David Brown, in Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on 4:23, says the call is given there a second time.

cites.quote: He begins ( Mar 4:3 ), with, Hearken, and concludes ( Mar 4:9 ) with, He that hath ears to hear, let him hear. … what he had said before he saith again, If any man have ears to hear, let him hear, Mar 4:23
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: If any man have ears to hear, let him hear--This for the second time on the same subject
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Blessed are you, four times
patterns.about: In Luke's account Jesus speaks to His disciples directly: blessed are you who are poor, who hunger now, who weep now, and when people hate you because of the Son of Man.
patterns.evidence: Adam Clarke, in his summary of Luke 6, says the Lord pronounces four blessings in verses 20 to 23 and four woes in verses 24 to 26.

cites.quote: Pronounces four blessings, Luk 6:20-23 , and four woes, Luk 6:24-26
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Four woes follow the four blessings
patterns.about: Right after the blessings come four woes: woe to the rich, to the well fed, to those who laugh now, and to those of whom all men speak well.
patterns.evidence: Adam Clarke, in his summary of Luke 6, says the Lord pronounces four blessings in verses 20 to 23 and four woes in verses 24 to 26.

cites.quote: Pronounces four blessings, Luk 6:20-23 , and four woes, Luk 6:24-26
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Love your enemies, said and said again
patterns.about: Jesus commands love for enemies, shows that loving only those who love you earns no credit, and then repeats the command: love your enemies, do good to them, and lend, expecting nothing in return.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Luke 6:27 to 35, notes that the command to love your enemies and do them good is repeated at verse 35.

cites.quote: This is repeated, Luk 6:35 : love your enemies, and do them good.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Do not fear men; fear Him
patterns.about: Jesus tells His friends not to be afraid of those who can only kill the body, then names three times in one verse the One to fear, and ends with do not be afraid, for you are worth more than many sparrows.
patterns.evidence: David Brown, in Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Luke 12:5, remarks how striking the repetition of fear Him is, since only the one fear will drive out the other.

cites.quote: Fear Him . . . Fear Him--how striking the repetition here! Only the one fear would effectually expel the other.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Pilate finds no guilt in Him, three times
patterns.about: Pilate tells the chief priests and the crowds that he finds no basis for a charge, says again that he found Him not guilty, and a third time that he found no offense worthy of death, yet gives Him up to their will.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, introducing Luke 23, speaks of Pilate's repeated testimonies to the innocence of Jesus before he yielded to the people.

cites.quote: Pilate's struggle with the people to release Jesus, his repeated testimonies concerning his innocency, but his yielding at length to their importunity
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: John came as a witness to testify
patterns.about: The opening of John's Gospel keeps coming back to the witness of John the Baptist. He came to testify about the Light, and the chapter gives his testimony again and again, ending with I have seen and testified.
patterns.evidence: Albert Barnes, on John 1:35, says the evangelist brings forward the clear and repeated testimony of John the Baptist and dwells on it, since it was impartial evidence that Jesus was the Messiah.

cites.quote: To do this, he adduces the decided and repeated testimony of John the Baptist. This was impartial evidence in the case, and hence he so particularly dwells upon
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Grace upon grace
patterns.about: The Word was full of grace and truth, from His fullness we have all received grace upon grace, and grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. Grace comes four times in four verses.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on John 1:16, says grace is a gift to be spoken of with emphasis, and that it is repeated: grace for grace.

cites.quote: this is a gift to be spoken of with an emphasis. It is repeated, grace for grace
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Truly, truly, I tell you
patterns.about: In John's Gospel Jesus often opens a saying with truly said twice over, twenty-five times in all, marking what follows as weighty and certain.
patterns.evidence: Albert Barnes, on John 1:51, says the word often comes in this Gospel, and that when it is doubled it shows the speaker's sense of the weight and certainty of what he says.

cites.quote: It is often used in this gospel. When repeated it expresses the speaker's sense of the importance of what he is saying, and the "certainty" that it is as he affirms.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: I am the bread of life
patterns.about: After feeding the five thousand, Jesus speaks of bread again and again: the manna, the true bread from heaven, and Himself, the bread of life and the living bread that came down from heaven.
patterns.evidence: David Brown, in Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 6:48, notes that I am the bread of life is repeated from verse 35.

cites.quote: I am the bread of life--"As he that believeth in Me hath everlasting life, so I am Myself the everlasting Sustenance of that life." (Repeated from Joh 6:35 ).
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The bread that came down from heaven
patterns.about: Again and again Jesus says that He has come down from heaven, and the crowd repeats it back as they grumble. It sets Him apart from the manna their fathers ate in the wilderness.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on John 6, says the saying that He is the bread which came down from heaven is often repeated there, pointing to verses 33, 50, 51 and 58.

cites.quote: That he is the bread which came down from heaven; this is often repeated here, Joh 6:33 , Joh 6:50 , Joh 6:51 , Joh 6:58
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: I will raise him up at the last day
patterns.about: Four times in the teaching on the bread of life Jesus makes the same promise: I will raise him up at the last day. It stands beside the eternal life the believer already has.
patterns.evidence: David Brown, in Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 6:54, says the promise to raise him up at the last day is repeated there for the fourth time, after verses 39, 40 and 44.

cites.quote: and I will raise him up at the last day--For the fourth time this is repeated (see Joh 6:39-40 , Joh 6:44 )
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: How were your eyes opened?
patterns.about: After Jesus heals the man born blind, his neighbors and then the Pharisees keep asking how his eyes were opened, his parents say they do not know who opened them, and the man answers that no one has ever done such a thing.
patterns.evidence: David Brown, in Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 9:26, says the Pharisees asked again what Jesus did and how He opened his eyes, hoping to trap him by repeated questions.

cites.quote: Then said they . . . again, What did he to thee? &c.--hoping by repeated questions to ensnare him
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Glorify, five times in two verses
patterns.about: When Judas has gone out, Jesus says that now the Son of Man is glorified and God is glorified in Him, and that God will glorify Him at once. The word comes five times in two verses.
patterns.evidence: David Brown, in Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 13:31, notes that in five brief clauses Jesus uses the word glorify five times.

cites.quote: And what is very remarkable, in five brief clauses He repeats this word "glorify" five times
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Remain in Me, and I will remain in you
patterns.about: In the picture of the vine and the branches, Jesus calls His disciples again and again to remain in Him and in His love, for no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on John 15:1 to 8, says the duty this picture teaches is to bear fruit, and to that end to abide in Christ.

cites.quote: II. The duty taught us by this similitude, which is to bring forth fruit, and, in order to this, to abide in Christ.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Bear much fruit
patterns.about: The Father prunes every branch that bears fruit so that it bears more, and the branch that remains in the vine bears much fruit. Jesus ends by saying He chose them to go and bear fruit that will remain.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on John 15:1 to 8, says the duty this picture teaches is to bear fruit. Albert Barnes, on John 15:16, says bearing fruit is the great end for which Christians are chosen.

cites.quote: II. The duty taught us by this similitude, which is to bring forth fruit, and, in order to this, to abide in Christ.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: It may be added that this is the great end for which Christians are chosen.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Love one another as I have loved you
patterns.about: Jesus speaks of the Father's love for Him and His love for them, and gives the command to love one another twice, in verse 12 and in verse 17, with the greatest love of all between them.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on John 15:12 to 17, notes the command to love one another is given at verse 12 and again at verse 17, and says no duty is more often pressed by the Lord than love for one another.

cites.quote: this is his commandment, that we love one another, Joh 15:12 , and again, Joh 15:17 . No one duty of religion is more frequently inculcated, nor more pathetically urged upon us, by our Lord Jesus, than that of mutual love
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Glorify Your Son, that Your Son may glorify You
patterns.about: Jesus begins His prayer by asking the Father to glorify Him, and asks it again in verse 5, with the glory He had before the world existed. Between the two, He says He has glorified the Father on earth.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on John 17:1 to 5, says Christ's one petition for himself, glorify me, is put up twice, because it looks both forward and back.

cites.quote: But this one petition, Glorify thou me, is twice put up, because it has a double reference.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: That they may be one as We are one
patterns.about: Jesus prays that His disciples, and those who will believe through their message, may be one as He and the Father are one, so that the world may believe that the Father sent Him.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on John 17:20 to 23, notes that the oneness of the Father and the Son is mentioned again and again in the prayer, at verse 11 and verses 21 to 23.

cites.quote: The oneness that is between the Father and the Son, which is mentioned again and again, Joh 17:11 , Joh 17:21-23 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: My kingdom is not of this world
patterns.about: Before Pilate, Jesus speaks of His kingdom three times in one answer, and of His servants, each time with an emphatic my, setting His kingdom apart from this world.
patterns.evidence: David Brown, in Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 18:36, notes that my comes four times in the verse, three times of His kingdom and once of His servants, each in the emphatic form.

cites.quote: It is worthy of notice that the "MY," which occurs four times in this one verse--thrice of His kingdom, and once of His servants--is put in the emphatic form
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Do you love Me? asked three times
patterns.about: By the fire Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves Him, after Peter had denied Him three times, and each time gives him a charge over His lambs and sheep. Two Greek words for love are used, both given as love.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on John 21:15 to 17, notes Christ asks Peter three times whether he loves Him. Adam Clarke, on verse 15, ties the threefold confession to the threefold denial. David Brown, in Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on verse 16, speaks of the question being repeated.

cites.quote: Three times Christ asks Peter whether he loves him or no.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Peter had thrice denied his Lord, and now Christ gives him an opportunity in some measure to repair his fault by a triple confession.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: In this repetition of the question, though the wound was meant to be reopened, the words "more than these" are not repeated
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The Way, a name for the faith
patterns.about: In Acts the followers of Jesus are those who belong to the Way. Saul hunts them, some at Ephesus malign the Way, a riot breaks out over it, and Paul tells Felix he worships God according to the Way.
patterns.evidence: Albert Barnes, on Acts 24:22, says that this way means the Christian religion, and that Luke uses the expression repeatedly for the Christian teaching.

cites.quote: Of that way - Of the Christian religion. This expression is repeatedly used by Luke to denote the Christian doctrine.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Be strong comes four times in Joshua's call
patterns.about: As Joshua takes up the work of Moses, the LORD tells him three times to be strong and courageous, and the people close the chapter by saying it to him once more. The charge carries the whole chapter.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Joshua 1:6-9, notes that the charge is given again and again and that God repeats it so often because Joshua distrusted his own strength. Keil and Delitzsch, on Joshua 1:9, note that the Lord repeats His call to firmness.

cites.quote: Be strong and of a good courage. And again ( Jos 1:7 ), as if this was the one thing needful: Only be strong and very courageous. And he concludes with this ( Jos 1:9 ): Be strong and of a good courage ... and therefore God repeats this so often
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: In conclusion, the Lord not only repeats His exhortation to firmness, but the promise that He gave in Jos 1:5 and Jos 1:6 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Serve rings through Joshua's last charge
patterns.about: At Shechem Joshua calls the people to choose whom they will serve, and the word comes again and again as he warns them and they answer more than once that they will serve the LORD.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Joshua 24:21-24, notes that the people make their resolve to serve the Lord and then repeat it. Keil and Delitzsch, on Joshua 24:24, speak of the people's repeated declaration that they will serve the Lord.

cites.quote: in the strength of divine grace we are resolved that we will serve the Lord." This resolution they repeat with an explication ( Jos 24:24 ): "The Lord our God will we serve
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: On the repeated and decided declaration of the people, "the Lord our God will we serve, and to His voice will we hearken," Joshua completed the covenant with them that day.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Each round in Judges opens with Israel doing evil
patterns.about: Seven times Judges says that the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD, and each time a new round of oppression and rescue begins. The same words mark each turn of the book's cycle.
patterns.evidence: Albert Barnes, on Judges 2:11, says this phrase for falling into idolatry comes seven times in Judges, once for each falling away. Matthew Henry, on Judges 13:1, notes that Israel did evil as they had done before, an account met with often already.

cites.quote: this is the regular phrase for falling into idolatry. It occurs seven times in Judges, as descriptive of the seven apostasies of Israel
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: a short account, such as we have too often met with already, of the great distress that Israel was in, which gave occasion for the raising up of a deliverer. They did evil, as they had done, in the sight of the Lord
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: No king in Israel frames the last stories
patterns.about: The closing chapters of Judges say four times that in those days there was no king in Israel, twice adding that everyone did what was right in his own eyes. The words frame the dark stories that end the book.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Judges 17:6, point to the remark that comes in both closing accounts, that there was no king in Israel. Matthew Henry, on Judges 21:25, calls the last verse a repetition of the cause of these disorders.

cites.quote: the remark, which occurs in both appendices, that at that time there was no king in Israel, and every one did what was right in his own eyes ( Jdg 17:6 ; Jdg 21:25 ).
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: A repetition of the cause of these confusions, Jdg 21:25 . Though God was their King, every man would be his own master, as if there was no king.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Hannah's asking and giving share one word
patterns.about: Hannah asks the LORD for a son and names him Samuel because she asked for him. When she gives the boy back, the word for dedicating him is the same Hebrew word, so the child asked of God is given to God.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on 1 Samuel 1:28, notes that Hannah gives Samuel back with the same word she used when she asked for him. Adam Clarke, on the same verse, notes that her words point back to her vow and that the verb for asked and for giving him is the same.

cites.quote: she uses this word Shaol, lent, because it is the same word that she had used before ( Sa1 1:20 , I asked him of the Lord), only in another conjugation.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: There is here a continual reference to her vow, and to the words which she used in making that vow. ... his mother said, Sa1 1:27 , The Lord hath given me my petition, which ... Shaalti, I Asked of him. In Sa1 1:28 she says: ... he shall be Lent unto the Lord: here we find the verb is the same
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The LORD calls the boy Samuel again and again
patterns.about: The word call runs through the night scene. The LORD calls, the boy runs to Eli thinking he called, and it happens again until Eli sees that the LORD is calling the boy.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on 1 Samuel 3:6-9, notes that the same call was repeated a second and third time.
