cites.quote: The same call was repeated, and the same mistake made, a second and third time, Sa1 3:6-9 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: But the same thing was repeated a second and a third time
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He is thrice called by the Lord
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: David would build God a house; God builds his
patterns.about: David wants to build a house for the LORD. The LORD answers that He will make David a house, a line of kings, and that David's son will build the house for His Name. The one word turns between temple and family.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on 2 Samuel 7:11, notes that David meant to build God a house and God in return promises to build him a house. Adam Clarke, on the same verse, sets the two houses side by side. Keil and Delitzsch, on 2 Samuel 7:5-16, see in it the truth that God builds a man's house before the man builds God's.

cites.quote: David had purposed to build God a house, and, in requital, God promises to build him a house, Sa2 7:11 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Thou hast in thy heart to make me a house; I have it in my heart to make thee a house
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: contains the deep general truth that God must first of all build a man's house, before the man can build God's house
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Forever is said three times of David's throne
patterns.about: In the promise to David the word forever comes once for his son's throne and twice more in the closing words about David's house, kingdom and throne.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on 2 Samuel 7:13-16, notes that forever is said in verse 13 and again and a third time in verse 16. Albert Barnes, on 2 Samuel 7:16, notes that forever is said twice there with emphasis.

cites.quote: But the establishing of his house, and his throne, and his kingdom, for ever ( Sa2 7:13 , and again, and a third time Sa2 7:16 . for ever)
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The words forever, emphatically twice repeated in Sa2 7:16 , show very distinctly that this prophecy looks beyond the succession of the kings of Judah of the house of David
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: In this telling too, God answers with a house for David
patterns.about: As in Samuel, David wants to build a house for the LORD, and the LORD answers that He will build David a house and that David's son will build Him one. The chapter turns on the one word.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, opening 1 Chronicles 17, divides the chapter between David's purpose to build God a house and God's promise to build David a house.

cites.quote: God's gracious acceptance of David's purpose to build him a house, and the promise he made thereupon ( Ch1 17:1-15 ). II. David's gracious acceptance of God's good promise to build him a house
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: David cries his dead son's name again and again
patterns.about: When David hears that Absalom is dead, he weeps and cries his son's name over and over, and he is still crying it out when the army comes home.
patterns.evidence: Adam Clarke, on 2 Samuel 19:4, agrees with Calmet that crying the dead one's name again and again belongs to the speech of mourning.

cites.quote: Calmet has properly remarked that the frequent repetition of the name of the defunct, is common in the language of lamentation.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Elisha swears three times not to leave Elijah
patterns.about: Three times Elijah asks Elisha to stay behind, and three times Elisha answers with the same double oath, by the life of the LORD and of Elijah himself, that he will not leave him.
patterns.evidence: Albert Barnes, on 2 Kings 2:2, calls the double oath, sworn three times in these verses, very remarkable.

cites.quote: This double oath, repeated three times Kg2 2:4 , Kg2 2:6 , is very remarkable.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Peace is asked about again and again as Jehu rides
patterns.about: As Jehu drives toward Jezreel, one rider and then a second asks whether he comes in peace, and then King Joram asks it too. Each time Jehu's answer turns the word back on the one who asks.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on 2 Kings 9:17-19, notes that each messenger asked the same question about peace and each had the same answer.

cites.quote: Each messenger asked the same question: "Is it peace? are you for us or for our adversaries? Do you bring good tidings or bad?" Each had the same answer: What hast thou to do with peace?
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Do not worship other gods is said three times
patterns.about: Recalling the covenant, the writer says three times that Israel must not worship other gods, and calls them to worship the LORD alone. The Hebrew word here is the word for fear.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on 2 Kings 17:35-38, notes that the covenant's great article, that they should not fear other gods, is said three times here.

cites.quote: especially that great article of it which is here thrice repeated, because it had been so often inculcated and so much insisted on, that they should not fear other gods.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The hand of God is on Ezra's whole journey
patterns.about: Ezra's account keeps saying that the hand of his God was upon him: when the king grants his requests, when he arrives, when Levites are found and when they are kept safe on the road.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Ezra 7:6, note that this expression comes in Ezra 7:9, 7:28, 8:18, 8:22 and 8:31 and twice in Nehemiah. Albert Barnes, on Ezra 7:6, calls it a favorite phrase of Ezra and Nehemiah.

cites.quote: The peculiar expression ... which is found only here and in Ezr 7:9 , Ezr 7:28 , Ezr 8:18 ; Neh 2:8 , Neh 2:18 , and in a slightly altered guise in Ezr 8:22 , Ezr 8:31 , "according to the good hand of his God, which was over him,"
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The use of this phrase in a good sense is rare elsewhere (compare Kg1 18:46 ), but is a favorite one with both Ezra and Nehemiah
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Nehemiah asks God again and again to remember
patterns.about: As Nehemiah tells of his last reforms, he breaks off again and again to ask God to remember him for good, and once to remember those who defiled the priesthood.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Nehemiah 13:31, speak of this often repeated prayer, pointing also to Nehemiah 13:14, 13:22 and 5:19.

cites.quote: On this frequently-repeated supplication (comp. Neh 13:14 , Neh 13:22 , and Neh 5:19 )
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Destroy, kill and annihilate: Haman's words return
patterns.about: Haman's decree orders the Jews to be destroyed, killed and annihilated. When Esther pleads with the king she names the same three Hebrew words, and the second decree gives the Jews the same words against their enemies.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Esther 7:4, notes that Esther refers to the words of the decree in Esther 3:13. Adam Clarke, on Esther 7:4, says she repeats the words of Haman's decree, and on Esther 8:11 that the new decree uses the same words.

cites.quote: She refers to the words of the decree ( Est 3:13 ), which aimed at nothing short of their destruction
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: To be destroyed, to be slain - She here repeats the words which Haman put into the decree. See Est 3:13 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: To destroy, to slay, and to cause to perish - The same words as in Haman's decree
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Good, seven times, then very good
patterns.about: Each day's work is weighed with the same word: God saw that it was good. The word comes seven times, and at the close of the sixth day it rises to very good, leaving no room for anything evil in what God made.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Genesis 1:31, note the word good applied to all God made and repeated with very at the close. Matthew Henry, on the same verse, notes it was said of each day's work but the second, and now very good.

cites.quote: By the application of the term "good" to everything that God made, and the repetition of the word with the emphasis "very" at the close of the whole creation, the existence of anything evil in the creation of God is absolutely denied
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Of each day's work (except the second) it was said that it was good, but now, it is very good.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Each according to its kind, ten times
patterns.about: As plants, sea creatures, birds and land animals are made, the same phrase marks each one: according to its kind. It comes ten times, and when the land animals are made it is said again over every class of them.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Genesis 1:24-25, note that the phrase after its kind covers each class of land creature and is repeated with every class when God's word is carried out.

cites.quote: "After its kind:" this refers to all three classes of living creatures, each of which had its peculiar species; consequently in Gen 1:25 , where the word of God is fulfilled, it is repeated with every class.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The ground, cursed and returned to
patterns.about: The sentence on Adam turns on the ground: it is cursed because of him, he will toil over it until he returns to it, and once sent out of the garden he must work the ground he was taken from.
patterns.evidence: James G. Murphy, in the Genesis part of Barnes' Notes, on Genesis 3:17-19, calls the soil the key word in the sentence on the man, and goes on to explain the curse on it.

cites.quote: The keyword in the sentence of the man is the "soil."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: His brother, said again and again
patterns.about: From Abel's birth to Cain's sentence the account keeps naming Abel as Cain's brother, seven times in all, so that the murder is seen for what it is: a man killing his own brother.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Genesis 4:8, say the writer repeats his brother again and again on purpose, to bring out the horror of the sin.

cites.quote: The writer intentionally repeats again and again the words "his brother," to bring clearly out the horror of the sin.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Canaan a servant, three times over
patterns.about: Noah's words over his sons keep coming back to one word: Canaan is to be a servant, to his brothers, to Shem, to Japheth. It returns like a refrain after each blessing.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Genesis 9:26, say Canaan's servitude comes in like a refrain beside both brothers. James G. Murphy, in the Genesis part of Barnes' Notes, on 9:26, also calls the line about Canaan as servant a refrain.

cites.quote: In contrast with the curse, the blessings upon Shem and Japhet are introduced with a fresh "and he said," whilst Canaan's servitude comes in like a refrain and is mentioned in connection with both his brethren
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Then follows the refrain, "And Kenaan shall be servant unto them."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Our father, again and again
patterns.about: In the account of Lot's daughters the word father comes eleven times, and the older son's name, Moab, may echo the words from father.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Genesis 19:37, say the name Moab likely means from the father, a reading made probable by the repeated words of our father and by their father.

cites.quote: rendered probable by the reiteration of the words "of our father" and "by their father"
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: This is the account of, heading each part
patterns.about: Genesis is laid out under one repeated heading, this is the account of, which opens the story of the heavens and the earth, then of Adam, Noah, Noah's sons, Shem, Terah, Ishmael, Isaac, Esau and Jacob.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Genesis 2:4, note the formula comes ten times in Genesis, always as a heading. James G. Murphy, in the Genesis part of Barnes' Notes, on 11:27, says the customary phrase marks the start of a new section.

cites.quote: in every other passage, in which the formula "these (and these) are the tholedoth" occurs (viz., ten times in Genesis; also in Num 3:1 ; Rut 4:18 ; Ch1 1:29 ), it is used as a heading
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This passage forms the commencement of the sixth document, as is indicated by the customary phrase, "These are the generations."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The stone on the well's mouth
patterns.about: At the well near Haran the stone over its mouth is named five times: the shepherds wait for all the flocks before rolling it away, but Jacob, on seeing Rachel, rolls it away himself.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Genesis 29:2-3, notes that the stone at the well's mouth is so often mentioned, and gives reasons it was kept there.

cites.quote: The stone at the well's mouth, which is so often mentioned here, was either to secure their property in it
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Pharaoh's heart hardened, again and again
patterns.about: Through the signs and plagues it is said again and again that Pharaoh's heart was hardened: ten times that the LORD hardened it, and just as often that Pharaoh hardened his own heart, until the sea.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Exodus 4:21, count ten places where the hardening is ascribed to God and just as many where Pharaoh hardened his own heart, using three Hebrew words for it; the main one is shown here.

cites.quote: The hardening of Pharaoh is ascribed to God, not only in the passages just quoted, but also in Exo 9:12 ; Exo 10:20 , Exo 10:27 ; Exo 11:10 ; Exo 14:8 ; that is to say, ten times in all … But it is also stated just as often, viz., ten times, that Pharaoh hardened his own heart
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: By the strength of His hand
patterns.about: In the chapter on the firstborn and the feast, Israel is told again and again that the LORD brought them out of Egypt by the strength of His hand, a mighty hand.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Exodus 13, bids readers observe how often the chapter says the LORD brought Israel out by strength of hand, and lists the four verses.

cites.quote: It must be observed how often it is said in this chapter that by strength of hand ( Exo 13:3 , Exo 13:14 , Exo 13:16 ), with a strong hand ( Exo 13:9 ), the Lord brought them out of Egypt.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Just as the LORD had commanded Moses
patterns.about: As the priests' garments are made and the tabernacle is set up, step after step closes with the same words: just as the LORD had commanded Moses. The work follows God's word exactly.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Exodus 39, notes that all six paragraphs on the holy garments end with these words, and on Exodus 40 that they are repeated seven times in under fourteen verses.

cites.quote: all the six paragraphs here, which give a distinct account of the making of these holy garments, conclude with those words, as the Lord commanded Moses
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: as before, so here it is repeated, as the Lord commanded Moses, seven times in less than fourteen verses.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The priests ordained as the LORD commanded
patterns.about: The ordination of Aaron and his sons is told step by step, and again and again a step ends with the words as the LORD had commanded, matching the orders given earlier.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Leviticus 8, says the rite agrees exactly with the orders in Exodus 29, and that, as with the tabernacle, as the LORD commanded Moses is repeated again and again.

cites.quote: Here, therefore, as in the account we had of the tabernacle and its vessels, it is again and again repeated, As the Lord commanded Moses.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Holy, again and again on the Day of Atonement
patterns.about: In the law for the Day of Atonement the word holy comes again and again: the Most Holy Place behind the veil, the Holy Place, and the holy linen garments Aaron must wear to go in.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Leviticus 16:3-4, say that in this chapter the word holy is often used in an emphatic sense, as of the Most Holy Place, so that the linen dress is marked as most holy.

cites.quote: in the present chapter the word kodesh, "holy," is frequently used in an emphatic sense (for example, in Lev 16:2 , Lev 16:3 , Lev 16:16 , of the most holy place of the dwelling), and by this predicate the dress is characterized as most holy.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: These words express the keynote to the whole book of Leviticus, being addressed to the whole nation.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Blood, the life, named again and again
patterns.about: The chapter keeps returning to blood: it is brought to the altar, it must never be eaten, for the life of the flesh is in the blood, and it is the blood that makes atonement.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Leviticus 17:10-14, says the ban on eating blood is repeated again and again here, with great stress laid on it.

cites.quote: The prohibition is repeated again and again, and reference had to the former laws to this purport … A great stress is laid upon it, as a law which has more in it than at first view one would think.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: I am the LORD your God, at start and close
patterns.about: The laws on marriage and purity open and close with the words I am the LORD your God, and say I am the LORD in between, so each command rests on who the LORD is to His people.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Leviticus 18:2, note the words I am the LORD your God placed at the head and repeated at the close. Samuel Clark, in the Leviticus part of Barnes' Notes, on 18:2, speaks of the frequent repetition of the formula in these laws.

cites.quote: By the words, "I am Jehovah your God," which are placed at the head and repeated at the close ( Lev 18:30 ), the observance of the command is enforced upon the people as a covenant obligation
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The frequent repetition of this formula in these parts of the Law may be intended to keep the Israelites in mind of their covenant with Yahweh in connection with the common affairs of life
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: I am the LORD, after command upon command
patterns.about: Command after command in this chapter ends with the same words, I am the LORD, or I am the LORD your God. Its laws on worship, the poor, the neighbor and the stranger all rest on that one name.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Leviticus 19, counts the words I am the LORD fifteen times in the chapter. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on 19:37, says these precepts are repeatedly sealed by that solemn word.

cites.quote: Here is the preface to the ten commandments, "I am the Lord," repeated fifteen times.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: I am the Lord--This solemn admonition, by which these various precepts are repeatedly sanctioned
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: My covenant, three times in one verse
patterns.about: When Israel confesses in exile, the LORD says He will remember His covenant with Jacob, with Isaac and with Abraham, naming it three times, and twice more holds to it.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Leviticus 26:42, says the word covenant is repeated three times to show that God is ever mindful of it.

cites.quote: The word covenant is thrice repeated, to intimate that God is ever mindful of it and would have us to be so.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The LORD named in each line of the blessing
patterns.about: The priests' blessing has three lines, and each names the LORD: may the LORD bless you, may the LORD make His face shine, may the LORD lift up His face. So His name is put on His people.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Numbers 6:24-26, note the name Jehovah repeated three times and see in it Father, Son and Spirit.

cites.quote: the name Jehovah is three times repeated in it
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The repetition of the name "Lord" or "Jehovah" three times, expresses the great mystery of the Godhead--three persons, and yet one God.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The cloud leads every move
patterns.about: These verses say again and again how the cloud ruled Israel's march: when it lifted they set out, where it settled they camped, whether for one night, a few days, a month or longer.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Numbers 9:15-23, says the cloud's moving and resting, and Israel marching and camping with it, is repeated again and again in these verses.

cites.quote: As long and as far as the cloud moved, so long and so far they marched … This is repeated again and again in these verses, because it was a constant miracle
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: He lifted up an oracle, four times
patterns.about: Balaam's last prophecy is cut into four by the same words, he lifted up an oracle: over Moab and Edom, then over Amalek, then the Kenites, and last the ships from Cyprus.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Numbers 24:15-24, say this last prophecy is divided into four by the fourfold repetition of the words he took up his oracle.

cites.quote: This prophecy is divided into four different prophecies by the fourfold repetition of the words, "he took up his parable" ( Num 24:15 , Num 24:20 , Num 24:21 , and Num 24:23 ).
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: They set out from, stage after stage
patterns.about: The record of Israel's journey from Egypt to the plains of Moab is told by the places they set out from, one stage after another, the same words opening almost every line.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Numbers 33:2-3, say the march is described by the places of departure, hence the constant repetition of the word they set out.

cites.quote: The march of the people is not described by the stations, or places of encampment, but by the particular spots from which they set out. Hence the constant repetition of the word … "and they broke up."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The place the LORD will choose
patterns.about: As Israel nears the land, the call to bring every offering only to the place the LORD will choose, and not to the high places of the nations, is pressed again and again through this chapter.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Deuteronomy 12, says the command to bring sacrifices to the one altar, and the ban on other places, is repeated again and again, as we teach children.

cites.quote: The command to do this, and the prohibition of the contrary, are here repeated again and again, as we teach children: and yet we are sure that there is in scripture no vain repetition
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The feasts kept where the LORD will choose
patterns.about: Passover, the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of Tabernacles are each tied to one place: the place the LORD will choose. The words come six times in these verses.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Deuteronomy 16, take up and affirm the count that the place the LORD will choose comes six times. T. E. Espin, in the Deuteronomy part of Barnes' Notes, on 16:1-16, says the point is repeated in various words six times in the first sixteen verses.

cites.quote: "the place which Jehovah thy God will choose" occurs six times ( Deu 16:2 , Deu 16:6 , Deu 16:7 , Deu 16:11 , Deu 16:15 , Deu 16:16 )
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: is reiterated in a variety of words no less than six times in the first sixteen verses of this chapter
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Justice, and justice alone
patterns.about: The charge to Israel's judges to judge with righteous judgment ends by saying the word twice over: pursue justice, and justice alone, so that you may live and possess the land.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Deuteronomy 16:20, say the repetition of the word justice is emphatic: justice and nothing but justice.

cites.quote: The repetition of the word justice is emphatic: justice, and nothing but justice
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Blessed, six times over
patterns.about: The blessings for obedience come in short lines, each saying blessed: in the city and the country, the fruit of womb and land, the basket and kneading bowl, coming in and going out.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Deuteronomy 28:3-6, say the fullness of God's blessing in every part of life is shown by a sixfold repetition of the word blessed.

cites.quote: In Deu 28:3-6 , the fulness of the blessing of God in all the relations of life is depicted in a sixfold repetition of the word "blessed."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Cursed, six times over, matching the blessings
patterns.about: The curses for disobedience answer the blessings line for line, each saying cursed: in the city and the country, the basket and kneading bowl, the fruit of womb and land, coming in and going out.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Deuteronomy 28:16-19, say the curse covers every part of life in a sixfold repetition of the word cursed, as the blessing did in 28:3-6.

cites.quote: the curse is proclaimed in all its extent, as covering all the relations of life, in a sixfold repetition of the word "cursed" ( Deu 28:16-19 , as above in Deu 28:3-6 )
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: In the siege and distress, three times
patterns.about: The darkest curse, of parents eating their own children, is told in three lines that each end the same way: in the siege and distress that your enemy will inflict on you.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Deuteronomy 28:53, say the words in the siege and in the straitness come back as a refrain, with an appalling sound, in verses 55 and 57.

cites.quote: This horrible distress is depicted still more fully in Deu 28:54-57 , where the words, "in the siege and in the straitness," etc. ( Deu 28:53 ), are repeated as a refrain, with their appalling sound, in Deu 28:55 and Deu 28:57 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The LORD your God, again and again
patterns.about: The promise of return after exile keeps naming God as the LORD your God: the one they turn back to, who gathers them, circumcises their hearts and makes them abound, is still their own God.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Deuteronomy 30:1-10, notes that Moses calls God the LORD your God twelve times in these ten verses, to encourage those who return to Him.

cites.quote: It is observable how Moses here calls God the Lord thy God twelve times in these ten verses, intimating, (1.) That penitents may take direction and encouragement in their return to God from their relation to him.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: God the Rock, again and again in the song
patterns.about: Moses' song calls God the Rock again and again: His work is perfect, Israel scorned the Rock of its salvation, and the enemies' rock is not like ours. The name holds up God's steadfast strength.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Deuteronomy 32:4, says God is called the Rock six times in this chapter. T. E. Espin, in the Deuteronomy part of Barnes' Notes, on the same verse, says the title is repeated five times in the song to set forth God's unchanging strength.

cites.quote: He is the rock. So he is called six times in this chapter
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This epithet, repeated no less than five times in the Song Deu 32:15 , Deu 32:18 , Deu 32:30-31 , represents those attributes of God which Moses is seeking to enforce, immutability and impregnable strength.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: God gave them over, said three times
patterns.about: Three times Paul says that God gave them over or up: to impurity, to dishonorable passions, and to a depraved mind. Each step away from God is met by the same words of judgment.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Romans 1:24-28, notes that the words He gave them up come three times here, in verses 24, 26 and 28, and calls this a spiritual judgment.

cites.quote: He gave them up; it is thrice repeated here, Rom 1:24 , Rom 1:26 , Rom 1:28 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Credited, again and again through Romans 4
patterns.about: The chapter turns on one word: Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness. Paul comes back to credited, counted and credits eleven times, from Abraham and David to all who believe.
patterns.evidence: Adam Clarke, in his closing notes on Romans 4, observes that the chapter says again and again that faith is credited for righteousness.

cites.quote: It is repeatedly said that Faith is imputed for righteousness
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The one trespass, named again and again
patterns.about: Through Romans 5:15-20 Paul keeps naming the trespass of the one man and sets it each time against the gift of grace that came through the one man, Jesus Christ.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on Romans 5:20, note that the offense is named four times in this section besides verse 20, and take it to mean the one first offense of Adam.

cites.quote: Throughout all this section "the offense" (four times repeated besides here) has one definite meaning, namely, "the one first offense of Adam"
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Righteousness, the word Romans keeps returning to
patterns.about: From the gospel that reveals the righteousness of God in 1:17 to the righteousness that comes by faith in chapter 10, Paul uses the word righteousness again and again to say how God makes people right with Himself.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on Romans 8:4, speak of the word so often used in this letter for the righteousness that justifies, listing 1:17, 3:21, 4:5-6 and 5:17-21. Barnes, on Romans 8:10, says the word is so frequently used in Romans for God's plan of justification.

cites.quote: the word so often used in this Epistle to denote "the righteousness which justifies" ( Rom 1:17 ; Rom 3:21 ; Rom 4:5-6 ; Rom 5:17-18 , Rom 5:21 )
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: I understand the expression to be used in the sense in which the word is so frequently used in this Epistle, as denoting God's plan of justification
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Christ named ten times in ten verses
patterns.about: In the opening of the letter Paul names Christ in almost every verse, ten times in all, before he turns to the divisions in the church, to point the quarreling believers to Christ alone.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on 1 Corinthians 1:10, say Paul wishes Christ to be all in all to the Corinthians and so names Him so often in this chapter.

cites.quote: by . . . Christ--whom Paul wishes to be all in all to the Corinthians, and therefore names Him so often in this chapter.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: All of them, five times over
patterns.about: All were under the cloud, all passed through the sea, all were baptized, all ate, all drank. The word all comes five times, and then verse 5 says that God was not pleased with most of them.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on 1 Corinthians 10:1-5, note that all is repeated five times for the five gifts God gave Israel, set against the many who fell in verse 5.

cites.quote: Five times the "all" is repeated, in the enumeration of the five favors which God bestowed on Israel ( Co1 10:1-4 ).
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: If Christ has not been raised, said again
patterns.about: Paul presses one point by saying it again: if the dead are not raised, then Christ has not been raised. Raised comes ten times in these verses, until verse 20 answers, Christ has indeed been raised.
patterns.evidence: Barnes, on 1 Corinthians 15:16, says the verse repeats verse 13 because of its importance: if there is no resurrection, the Lord Jesus was not raised.

cites.quote: This is a repetition of what is said in Co1 15:13 . It is repeated here, evidently, because of its importance. It was a great and momentous truth which would "bear" repetition, that if there was no resurrection, as some held, then it would follow that the Lord Jesus was not raised up.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Victory, three times at the close
patterns.about: Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O Death, is your victory? Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory. The word comes three times as the chapter on the resurrection ends.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on 1 Corinthians 15:57, say the repetition of the word victory from verses 54 and 55 fits the triumph that has been won.

cites.quote: The repetition of the word ( Co1 15:54-55 ) is appropriate to the triumph gained.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Comfort, ten times in five verses
patterns.about: The God of all comfort comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort others with the comfort we have received. Comfort and comforted come again and again in these five verses, and comfort stands out more in this letter than in the first.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on 2 Corinthians 1:5, say comfort is more prominent in this letter than in the first one to Corinth.

cites.quote: Comfort preponderates in this Epistle above that in the first Epistle
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The name Jesus, again and again
patterns.about: In these verses Paul names Jesus nine times: we carry around the death of Jesus so that the life of Jesus may be revealed in our body. The name stands by itself in the middle of his sufferings.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on 2 Corinthians 4:10, note that the name Jesus by itself is often repeated here, as if Paul felt its sweetness amid his sufferings.

cites.quote: The name "Jesus," by itself is often repeated here as Paul seems, amidst sufferings, peculiarly to have felt its sweetness.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Weakness, the word Paul boasts in
patterns.about: From who is weak, and I am not weak, through My power is perfected in weakness, to He was crucified in weakness, Paul keeps coming back to weakness, because there the power of Christ rests on him.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on 2 Corinthians 12:9, say Paul often repeats the word weakness in the eleventh, twelfth and thirteenth chapters, as being Christ's own word to him.

cites.quote: Paul often repeats the word "weakness" or "infirmity" (the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth chapters) as being Christ's own word.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: In the heavenly realms, four times
patterns.about: The heavenly realms are where God has blessed us in Christ, where Christ is seated, where we are seated with Him, and where the rulers learn the wisdom of God. The phrase comes four times in three chapters.
patterns.evidence: Barnes, on Ephesians 1:3, notes that the phrase comes again in 1:20, 2:6 and 3:10, and finds it remarkable that it comes in the same short form four times in this one letter.

cites.quote: The same phrase occurs again in Eph 2:6 ; Eph 3:10 ; and it is remarkable that it should occur in the same elliptical form four times in this one epistle, and, I believe, in no other part of the writings of Paul.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Joy and rejoice, all through Philippians
patterns.about: Written in chains, the letter keeps returning to joy: I pray with joy, I rejoice, make my joy complete, rejoice in the Lord always. Joy and rejoice run through all four chapters.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on Philippians 1:4, call joy the mark of this letter, as love is of Ephesians, and list 1:18, 2:2, 2:19, 2:28, 3:1, 4:1 and 4:4.

cites.quote: with joy--the characteristic feature in this Epistle, as love is in that to the Ephesians
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: All of you, said again and again
patterns.about: In the opening verses Paul keeps saying all: to all the saints, in every prayer for all of you, it is right for me to feel this way about all of you, I long for all of you. No one in the church is left out.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on Philippians 1:4, note the frequent repetition in this letter of all with you, showing that Paul loves them all alike and will not recognize divisions among them.

cites.quote: for you all--The frequent repetition in this Epistle of "all" with "you," marks that Paul desires to declare his love for all alike, and will not recognize any divisions among them.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: You know, said again and again
patterns.about: Paul keeps reminding the believers of what they saw for themselves: you know what kind of men we were, you know our coming was not in vain, you know we are destined for trials.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on 1 Thessalonians 3:4, say the repetition of you know, so often, is an argument: being warned before of trouble, they should be less easily shaken by it.

cites.quote: The repetition of "ye know," so frequently, is designed as an argument, that being forewarned of coming affliction, they should be less readily "moved" by it.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Rest, the word the warning turns on
patterns.about: They shall never enter My rest, from the psalm, is taken up again and again: God rested on the seventh day, Joshua had not given them rest, and so a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God.
patterns.evidence: Barnes, on Hebrews 4, says the writer appeals to the places in the Old Testament where the word rest occurs, to show that a rest still remains for believers.

cites.quote: Addressing Hebrew Christians, he, of course, appeals to the Old Testament, and refers to several places where the word "rest" occurs, and argues that those expressions are of such a character as to show that there remains a "rest" for Christians yet.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Conscience, the thing the old gifts could not cleanse
patterns.about: The gifts and sacrifices could not cleanse the conscience of the worshiper, but the blood of Christ purifies our consciences. The word comes in 9:9, 9:14, 10:2 and 10:22.
patterns.evidence: Adam Clarke, closing his notes on Hebrews 9, points to the word conscience as one that occurs so often in this chapter and in other parts of the letter.

cites.quote: On the word conscience, which occurs so often in this chapter, and in other parts of this epistle
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Living, a word this letter loves
patterns.about: A living hope, the living and enduring word of God, the living Stone, and you as living stones. The word living comes again and again as the letter opens.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on 1 Peter 1:3, call living a favorite word of Peter, pointing to 1:23 and 2:4-5, and say he delights in life overcoming death in the believer.

cites.quote: Living is a favorite expression of Peter ( Pe1 1:23 ; Pe1 2:4-5 ). He delights in contemplating life overcoming death in the believer.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Hope, a mark of this letter
patterns.about: The letter opens with a living hope and keeps returning to it: set your hope fully on grace, your faith and hope are in God, be ready to give the reason for the hope that is in you.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, in their opening to 1 Peter, call glory and hope prominent features of the letter, and on 1:13 note that hope is repeated from 1:3.

cites.quote: Glory and hope are prominent features in this Epistle
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: "Hope" is repeated from Pe1 1:3 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Suffering, in every chapter
patterns.about: Suffering for doing good, Christ suffered for you, if you should suffer for what is right, share in the sufferings of Christ. The letter keeps speaking to believers as people who suffer.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on 1 Peter 4:12, notes that counsel and comfort for believers as sufferers is repeated in every chapter of the letter, because persecution was their greatest danger.

cites.quote: The frequent repetition of counsel and comfort to Christians, considered as sufferers, in every chapter of this epistle, shows that the greatest danger these new converts were in arose from the persecutions to which their embracing Christianity exposed them.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Knowledge of the Lord, through 2 Peter
patterns.about: Grace and peace through the knowledge of God, all we need through the knowledge of Him, add to virtue knowledge, and at the end, grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord. The letter opens and closes with it.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, opening 2 Peter, call full knowledge the mark of this letter, as hope is of the first; on 1:2 they say the knowledge of Jesus our Lord is the main aim of Peter's urging.

cites.quote: Hope is characteristic of the First Epistle; full knowledge, of the Second Epistle.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Still the prominent object of Peter's exhortation is "the knowledge of Jesus our Lord"
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Remain in Him, said again and again
patterns.about: Whoever claims to abide in Him, remain in the Son and in the Father, remain in Christ, God remains in us. The same word, abide or remain, runs through the heart of the letter.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, opening 1 John, list abide in Him among John's favorite words. Barnes, on 1 John 3:6, calls it quite a favorite word of John for being joined to Christ, listing places from 2:6 to 4:16.

cites.quote: Many terms which in the Gospel are given as Christ's, in the Epistle appear as the favorite expressions of John, naturally adopted from the Lord. Thus the contrasted terms, "flesh" and "spirit," "light" and "darkness," "life" and "death," "abide in Him"
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: In the writings of John, however, it is quite a favorite word to denote the relation which one sustains to another, in the sense of being united to him, or remaining with him in affection and love
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: God is light, and walking in the light
patterns.about: God is light; walk in the light as He is in the light; the true light is already shining; whoever loves his brother remains in the light. Light, set against darkness, carries the opening of the letter.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, opening 1 John, count light and darkness among the terms that are John's favorite words in this letter, taken over from the Lord.

cites.quote: Many terms which in the Gospel are given as Christ's, in the Epistle appear as the favorite expressions of John, naturally adopted from the Lord. Thus the contrasted terms, "flesh" and "spirit," "light" and "darkness,"
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Fellowship with God and with one another
patterns.about: So that you may have fellowship with us, and our fellowship is with the Father and with His Son. If we walk in the light, we have fellowship with one another. The word comes four times in five verses.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, opening 1 John, call fellowship with the Father and the Son, and with one another, a favorite phrase of John.

cites.quote: fellowship with the Father and Son, and with one another," is a favorite phrase also, not found in the Gospel, but in Acts and Paul's Epistles.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Keep His commandments, three times
patterns.about: We know Him if we keep His commandments; whoever says I know Him but does not keep them is a liar; whoever keeps His word has the love of God perfected in him.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on 1 John 2:3, call keep John's favorite word, used instead of do, meaning to watch over and guard as something precious.

cites.quote: keep--John's favorite word, instead of "do," literally, "watch," "guard," and "keep safe" as a precious thing
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: We know, three times at the close
patterns.about: The letter ends with three sure things, each begun with we know: anyone born of God does not keep on sinning, we are of God, and the Son of God has come.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on 1 John 5:18, say we know is repeated three times with emphasis, to press home the three truths it introduces.

cites.quote: We know--Thrice repeated emphatically, to enforce the three truths which the words preface, as matters of the brethren's joint experimental knowledge.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The Lamb, John's name for Christ in this book
patterns.about: From the Lamb who stood as if slain in chapter 5 to the throne of God and of the Lamb in chapter 22, the word for lamb comes twenty-nine times, and every time but one it names Christ.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, opening Revelation, count the word for Lamb twenty-nine times in the book, and find it only once elsewhere in the New Testament, in John 21:15.

cites.quote: The Greek diminutive for "Lamb" (arnion, literally, "lambkin") occurs twenty-nine times in the Apocalypse, and the only other place where it occurs is Joh 21:15 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Seven, through the whole book
patterns.about: Seven churches, seven spirits, seven lampstands and stars, seven seals, seven trumpets, seven angels with seven bowls. The number seven runs through the whole book.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on Revelation 1:4, say seven comes more often in this book than anywhere else in Scripture. Barnes, on 1:4, calls it a favorite number of the book and lists the seven letters, seals, trumpets and bowls.

cites.quote: In the Apocalypse, where God's covenant with His Church comes to its consummation, appropriately the number seven recurs still more frequently than elsewhere in Scripture.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The number seven is evidently a favorite number in the Book of Revelation
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The wound that was healed, told three times
patterns.about: One head of the beast had a mortal wound that was healed. The chapter says it again in verse 12 and again in verse 14, the beast that had been wounded by the sword and yet had lived.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on Revelation 13:3, note that wounded and healed are repeated twice more with emphasis, in verses 12 and 14.

cites.quote: wounded . . . healed--twice again repeated emphatically ( Rev 13:12 , Rev 13:14 )
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: To the one who overcomes, in every letter
patterns.about: Each of the seven letters to the churches closes with a promise to the one who overcomes, and the last ties it to Christ: just as I overcame and sat down with My Father on His throne.
patterns.evidence: Adam Clarke, on Revelation 3:21, notes that in every case the closing promise is made to the one who overcomes.

cites.quote: In every case it is to him that overcometh, to the conqueror, that the final promise is made.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: He who has an ear, in all seven letters
patterns.about: Every one of the seven letters says, He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches, so what is said to one church is meant for all of them.
patterns.evidence: Barnes, on Revelation 2:7, notes that this call comes at the close of each of the letters to the seven churches, and that it was a way of speaking used by the Lord in His ministry.

cites.quote: This expression occurs at the close of each of the epistles addressed to the seven churches
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Hallelujah, four times
patterns.about: As Babylon falls, heaven rings with Hallelujah: a great multitude, the elders and the living creatures, and then a voice like many waters. The word comes four times in six verses.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on Revelation 19:1, note that Hallelujah occurs four times in this passage.

cites.quote: "Hallelu-Jah" occurs four times in this passage.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: These words are faithful and true
patterns.about: Near the end the book says three times that its words are true: these are the true words of God, these words are faithful and true, and again, these words are faithful and true.
patterns.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, on Revelation 22:6, note that the saying these words are true is given three times, at 19:9, 21:5 and 22:6.

cites.quote: These sayings are true--thrice repeated ( Rev 19:9 ; Rev 21:5 ).
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: The Almighty, the name Job's speakers use for God
patterns.about: As Job and those who speak with him argue over why the righteous suffer, God is called the Almighty thirty-one times in the book, far more than His name the LORD in its speeches.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, in his introduction to Job, notes that God is called the Almighty above thirty times in the book.

cites.quote: He lived while God was known by the name of God Almighty more than by the name of Jehovah; for he is called Shaddai - the Almighty, above thirty times in this book.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Where can wisdom be found? asked twice
patterns.about: The chapter goes deep into the earth with the miner and finds every treasure but wisdom. The question where wisdom is found is asked and then asked again, until the end answers it: the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom.
patterns.evidence: Albert Barnes, on Job 28:20, says the question of verse 12 is repeated there to give it greater emphasis. Fausset, in Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on the same verse, says verse 12 is repeated with great force.

cites.quote: Whence then cometh wisdom? - This question is now repeated from Job 28:12 , in order to give it greater emphasis.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Job 28:12 repeated with great force.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: His voice: the thunder, again and again
patterns.about: Elihu bids Job listen to the thunder, and in four verses speaks of God's voice again and again. The storm is heard as God speaking, as in Psalm 29.
patterns.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Job 37, note the word voice repeated five times and compare the seven times in Psalm 29. Fausset, in Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Job 37:5, points to Psalm 29, where as here the voice of God is repeated.

cites.quote: The repetition of קול … five times calls to mind the seven קולות
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: See Psa 29:1-11 , where, as here, the "voice" of God is repeated with grand effect.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: He says to himself, three times
patterns.about: Three times the psalm lets the wicked man speak in his own heart: I will not be moved; God has forgotten; You will never call me to account. His pride comes out of what he tells himself.
patterns.evidence: Albert Barnes, on Psalm 10:13, says this saying in the heart is repeated there for the third time in the psalm, after verses 6 and 11.

cites.quote: He hath said in his heart - This expression is here repeated for the third time in the psalm. See Psa 10:6 , Psa 10:11 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: How long? four times
patterns.about: The psalm opens with one cry four times over: How long, O LORD? Forgotten, hidden from, sorrowing, pressed by an enemy, David asks how long, before he turns to trust and to sing.
patterns.evidence: Albert Barnes, on Psalm 13:1-2, takes each time the psalmist asks how long as one more side of his trouble, the fourth being the enemy over him.

cites.quote: How long - Referring to a second aspect or phase of his troubles. … How long shall mine enemy be exalted over me? - This is the fourth form or phase of his trouble, and he asks how long this was to continue.

patterns.short: The LORD in each line on His word
patterns.about: The first half of the psalm speaks of God in the skies. The second half praises His law and names Him by His own name, the LORD, in each line on His word, through to the closing prayer to the LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer.
patterns.evidence: Matthew Henry, on Psalm 19:7-9, notes the name Jehovah repeated in each of the six sentences on God's word. Keil and Delitzsch, introducing Psalm 19, note the covenant name used seven times in the second part.

cites.quote: in six sentences ( Psa 19:7-9 ), in each of which the name Jehovah is repeated, and no vain repetition, for the law has its authority and all its excellency from the law-maker.

patterns.short: The King of Glory, called for again and again

patterns.short: Ascribe to the LORD, three times
patterns.about: The psalm opens by calling the heavenly beings three times to ascribe to the LORD glory and strength, before the storm shows why.

patterns.short: Your loving devotion, at start and end

patterns.short: Each man is but a breath
patterns.about: David measures his days and finds a life no more than a breath. The thought comes back in the middle and at the close of the psalm: surely each man is but a vapor.

cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

patterns.short: Truly, surely: the psalm's small word

cites.quote: both describe the nothingness of everything human in the same language; both delight more than other Psalms in the use of the assuring, confident אך

patterns.short: Sing praises, five times over

patterns.evidence: Adam Clarke, on Psalm 47:6, notes that the word sing praises is repeated four times in that short verse, showing the people's earnestness and joy.

cites.quote: Sing praises - זמרו zammeru: this word is four times repeated in this short verse, and shows at once the earnestness and happiness of the people.

patterns.short: In God alone, again and again

cites.quote: The particle אך occurs there four times, and in this Psalm even as many as six times.

patterns.short: God blesses us, three times

cites.quote: Let the people praise thee, O God! let them have matter for praise, let them have hearts for praise … It is again repeated ( Psa 67:5 ) as that which the psalmist's heart was very much upon.

patterns.short: He is holy, three times

patterns.short: Bless the LORD, six times
patterns.about: David calls his own soul to bless the LORD, then angels, hosts and all God's works, and ends calling on his soul again. The call to bless runs through the whole psalm.

patterns.short: Then they cried out to the LORD

patterns.short: Let them give thanks to the LORD

patterns.evidence: Albert Barnes, introducing Psalm 107, says its design is shown in the words repeated in verses 8, 15, 21 and 31, the call to praise the Lord for His goodness.

patterns.short: Praise the LORD, over and over

patterns.short: He is their help and shield

patterns.short: I called on the name of the LORD

patterns.short: Give me understanding

cites.quote: In the petition "give me understanding" (which occurs six times in this Psalm)

patterns.short: Revive me, three times

patterns.short: Sing to the LORD, three times
